    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md
    available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks out).

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance and full
      access to Mosaic''s product set.

      - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic Relay
      holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new markets.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic has pass/fail
      results for everyone but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed at Mosaic''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
      launching close+1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.

      - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were already
      KYC''d.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail results
      exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for users onboarded
      before 2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic Relay''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

      - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic buys
      Harbor''s assets)

      - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another institution''s
      prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification required? — Not sure
      / need to check with compliance

      - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the last year?
      — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic Relay
      plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its own? — Use/assume
      Harbor''s licenses

      - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what is the
      plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification and recordkeeping
      obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits
      reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

      - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year been reviewed,
      and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed
      and remain in diligence.

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what is
      the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before onboarding
      those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses
      for the four new markets.


      ## Assumptions


      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and Harbor''s
      MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition without new
      state approval

      - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s
      own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

      - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and validated
      before close without a monitoring gap

      - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state MTL
      regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in 41 states
      (per the request).

      - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
      which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
      (structure not yet confirmed).'

        working_ask: Does the Harbor Pay acquisition migration require legal review
          before the Nov 15 close, and what legal workstreams must be addressed pre-close
          (money transmission licensing, KYC/BSA-AML, SAR/alerts handling, monitoring
          vendor transition, and the welcome bonus campaign)?
        issues:
        - 'Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under the
          combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer/survive
          the acquisition'
        - 'BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with missing underlying
          documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay''s independent CIP/AML
          obligations'
        - 'SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor''s
          ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability'
        - 'Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring when
          the SaaS contract terminates at close'
        - 'Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money transmission
          or consumer protection implications'
        open_questions:
        - Acquisition structure (asset vs. stock purchase) — determines whether Harbor's
          MTLs and regulatory obligations transfer to Mosaic Relay
        - Whether Harbor's state MTLs can be assumed/transferred or must be re-applied
          for in the four new markets
        - Whether Mosaic Relay's own AML program and CIP can lawfully rely on Harbor's
          prior KYC without re-verification
        - Details of the ~40 open alerts and SARs (nature, age, whether any are unresolved
          or reportable)
        - Whether the $50 welcome bonus is a deposit/interest-like offer implicating
          state money transmission or consumer protection rules
        public_research_questions:
        - State money transmitter license transfer/assumption requirements in an acquisition
          context
        - BSA/AML CIP obligations when relying on a prior financial institution's
          KYC in a merger/acquisition
        - Successor obligations for open SARs and alerts in an acquisition

    available_excerpt: '# Original Request


      From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
      close+1.

      Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs from
      the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


      Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.'

  content: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe Harbor Pay migration
    needs legal and compliance review before the planned Nov 15 close. This is the
    accepted working view. It is not a recorded decision.\n\nThis draft recommends
    separating the acquisition closing from the launch of regulated services. The
    asset purchase can proceed while Mosaic prepares for migration. However, Mosaic
    should not give all Harbor users full access on day one unless these conditions
    are met:\n\n1. Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close service in
    each affected state.\n2. Compliance confirms how Mosaic can use Harbor’s prior
    know-your-customer (KYC) results and remedy missing records.\n3. Authorized reviewers
    assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity report (SAR) history.\n4.
    Mosaic validates the replacement transaction-monitoring feed without a coverage
    gap.\n\nIf a condition is not met, Mosaic should hold the affected state launch,
    restrict affected accounts, or delay full product access. The planned $50 welcome
    bonus should wait until its structure, terms, and disclosures are reviewed.\n\nNo
    decision has been recorded.\n\n### Assumptions used\n\n- Harbor is a licensed
    money transmitter subject to applicable state and federal anti-money-laundering
    requirements. The licensing, KYC, alert, and monitoring answers depend on this
    unverified premise.\n- Mosaic will become the operating provider after close.
    This affects whether Harbor could remain the licensed provider during a transition.\n-
    This analysis does not assume that Harbor’s licenses transfer, that its KYC results
    satisfy Mosaic’s program, or that monitoring can continue without a gap.\n- Mosaic’s
    41-state license footprint is a reported fact. It is not treated as an assumption.\n-
    The acquisition is a reported asset purchase. The older assumption that its structure
    was unknown is superseded by that reported answer.\n\n### Record conflicts\n\n-
    Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states,
    and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states
    larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says the acquisition opens
    four new markets. This affects which states need separate authority or launch
    restrictions. The two license lists and the intended meaning of “market” are needed.\n-
    Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`. The reported close is “Nov
    15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake. A saved hypothetical uses
    November 15, 2026, but that does not establish the actual closing year. The operative
    close date and year remain unresolved.\n\n## Decision question\n\nDoes any part
    of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before the Nov 15 close?\n\n##
    Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045 -->\n### Money transmission
    licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under the combined 44-state footprint
    and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive the acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic
    should not treat Harbor’s money transmitter licenses as assets that automatically
    transfer in the asset purchase. Mosaic should not launch regulated services in
    a state without documented authority for its complete post-close activity.\n\nThe
    acquisition may close separately from the service launch. A state launch hold
    is the current fallback where authority is not established.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThe
    saved research concludes that the answer must be determined state by state. The
    review must cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction notices or approvals, interim
    operation, outstanding obligations, and Harbor’s license surrender.\n\nFour sources
    were retrieved, but no operative passage was read or verified. They do not establish
    the governing rule in any affected state:\n\n- [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
    [CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538-157583424427.md)\n-
    [New York Department of Financial Services licensing page — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4-fa80c95c5393.md)\n-
    [OCC commentary — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413-e75b998a6dec.md)\n-
    [Fenergo licensing overview — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200-fcb5e16956fb.md)\n\nThe
    model act is not proof of any specific state’s law. The premise that an asset
    purchase does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority remains
    an unverified state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor reportedly has
    licenses in 38 states. Mosaic reportedly has licenses in 41 states. Their combined
    footprint is reported as 44 states. Mosaic plans to use or assume Harbor’s licenses
    in the new markets.\n\nThe unified Mosaic account, combined balance, and access
    to Mosaic products suggest that Mosaic may become the actual service provider.
    If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or licenses active might not authorize Mosaic’s
    conduct.\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider during a transition only
    if the customer contracts, funds flow, operating control, licenses, bonds, records,
    and applicable state rules support that result. The structure must match actual
    operations.\n\nA partner bank holding funds would not by itself resolve the issue.
    The result still depends on who contracts with users, controls transfers, owes
    repayment, records balances, resolves errors, and performs the regulated duties.\n\n**Next
    step**\n\nIdentify the Harbor-only jurisdictions and complete one state matrix.
    It should address Mosaic’s authority, required filings and approvals, operation
    while an application is pending, transfer of customer obligations, bank custody
    and control, Harbor’s run-off duties, and the required launch restriction if authority
    is not established.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start
    -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved
    research snapshot. Its facts and assumptions may predate later records. Use the
    current answer above for application to the current matter.\n\nDo not rely on
    transferability without an applicable state rule, approval, or written regulator
    position.\n\nThe answer must be determined state by state and must cover more
    than technical change-of-control rules.\n\nThis path is possible only if Harbor
    remains the real provider and the relevant states permit the arrangement. The
    unified Mosaic account design may conflict with that position.\n\nThe result depends
    on the contracts and actual funds flow. Custody alone should not be treated as
    a licensing exemption or transfer mechanism.\n\nResearch saved. 4 sources retrieved;
    0 with passages read.\n\nNext step: Identify the four Harbor-only states and complete
    one matrix covering license authority, transaction filings, interim operation,
    bank custody, outstanding obligations, and license surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed
    analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical answer**\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money transmitter
    licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.** Use this closing
    rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated launch by Mosaic in that
    state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close. However, Mosaic should not activate
    regulated services in the four Harbor-only states unless one of these conditions
    is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own license.\n2. The state approves a transfer
    or other license change.\n3. The regulator confirms a lawful interim structure.\n4.
    Harbor remains the real licensed provider under a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic
    blocks regulated functions in that state.\n\nThe planned unified Mosaic account
    is important. It suggests that Mosaic, not Harbor, will become the service provider.
    If that is correct, keeping Harbor’s legal entity and licenses alive might not
    give Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No verified operative authority retrieved.**
    The collection found the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act and a
    New York regulator licensing page. However, no exact provision about an asset
    sale, license transfer, interim operation, or custody was available for review.
    Also, a model act is not proof of the law adopted in a specific state. The state-specific
    conclusions below remain conditional.\n\n**Work needed before launch**\n\n| Work
    | Why | Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n|
    Identify the four Harbor-only states | These states have the clearest authority
    gap | Licensing team | Now | Confirmed license list and covered activities | Block
    regulated functions in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every affected state
    | Transfer, notice, approval, and surrender rules can differ | State regulatory
    counsel | Before the closing conditions are final | Applicable rule, filing deadline,
    regulator response, and license status | Delay migration in the affected state
    |\n| Confirm the post-close service provider | The licensed entity must match
    the actual operating model | Product and deal counsel | Before customer notices
    and account design are final | Contracts, user interface, funds-flow diagram,
    and operating roles | Keep Harbor as the actual provider where permitted |\n|
    Review notices and approvals | An asset sale can create separate seller and buyer
    requirements | Licensing team | Before each state deadline | Filing receipts and
    required approvals or non-objections | Make approval a state launch condition
    |\n| Confirm interim operating authority | A pending application should not be
    assumed to permit operation | State regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable
    rule or written regulator confirmation | Keep Harbor customers segregated or restrict
    transactions |\n| Review partner-bank arrangements | Bank custody does not, by
    itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing position | Payments counsel and bank relationship
    owner | Before balances move | Bank agreements, account titles, control rights,
    reconciliation design, and bank consent | Keep funds and obligations in the existing
    structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and surrender plans | Harbor may retain
    duties for balances, claims, records, and reports | Harbor compliance and deal
    counsel | Before surrender or operational shutdown | Regulator-approved plan and
    continued bonds and financial coverage | Keep Harbor licensed and operational
    longer |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo not search only for a rule called
    “license transfer.” Review each state for:\n\n- sale of substantially all assets;\n-
    change of control;\n- change in business plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n-
    assignment of outstanding payment obligations;\n- change in responsible persons,
    locations, or agents;\n- license surrender or termination;\n- customer agreement
    assignment; and\n- movement of stored balances or customer funds.\n\nAn asset
    purchase might fall outside a technical “change of control” rule because Harbor’s
    ownership does not change. That does not resolve the issue. Harbor might still
    need a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might separately need authority before
    it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe state matrix should distinguish:\n\n-
    notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n- approval before customer migration;\n-
    new license required;\n- operation permitted while an application is pending;\n-
    regulator-approved transition available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n**Interim
    operation**\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for a transition period.
    However, the structure must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA supportable
    structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains responsible to
    customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n- Harbor controls the
    regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses, bonds, and financial coverage
    remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding obligations remain covered.\n-
    Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints, and examinations.\n- Required
    records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational role is permitted.\n- The partner
    bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant regulator permits or accepts the
    structure.\n\nThe present plan creates tension with this approach. A single Mosaic
    account, one combined balance, and full access to Mosaic products make it harder
    to show that Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank custody**\n\nA
    partner bank account is not automatically a substitute for a money transmitter
    license. The key questions concern the complete activity and obligation flow.\n\nFor
    each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1. Who receives the customer’s
    instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit or return the funds?\n3.
    In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is it a custodial or “for benefit
    of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6. Who owns the ledger and resolves
    errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer fails?\n8. Which entity owes the customer
    a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license, bond, and permissible investments cover
    the obligation?\n10. Does the bank agreement permit assignment, migration, or
    a change in the program manager?\n11. Is bank consent required before closing
    or migration?\n12. What happens to funds if Harbor, Mosaic, or the bank relationship
    ends?\n\nA bank-led model might provide a different licensing analysis if the
    bank is the actual provider and Mosaic performs only permitted services. A bank
    account that merely holds funds for Mosaic or Harbor is different. The legal documents,
    customer terms, control rights, and actual operations must all support the claimed
    model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n- account segregation;\n- daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls
    and reserve funding;\n- bank setoff rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n-
    continuity if the account is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n- return
    and chargeback duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures; and\n-
    whether any deposit-insurance statement is accurate for the actual account structure.\n\n**Recommended
    closing position**\n\nKeep the acquisition closing separate from the regulated-service
    launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic
    has documented authority. For overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing
    licenses cover the complete post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender
    Harbor’s licenses or release its bonds until the applicable regulators permit
    it and all outstanding obligations have been assigned, completed, or placed into
    an approved run-off structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change the current
    recommendation. It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody is part of
    the licensing analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch
    history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
    retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
    -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with missing
    underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's independent
    CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe current no-reverification plan
    is not ready for approval. Mosaic has not confirmed that its anti-money-laundering
    and customer identification program permits reliance on Harbor’s prior KYC. Pass/fail
    results alone may not provide the records or risk information that Mosaic needs.\n\nMosaic
    should not give an affected user unrestricted access unless compliance confirms
    that reliance is permitted and that the available records are sufficient, or a
    defined remediation process is complete.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue
    has not been researched. No saved authority establishes Mosaic’s precise federal
    duties or whether Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s checks after this asset purchase.\n\nThe
    unverified legal premise is that the entity providing the post-close financial
    service must follow its applicable customer identification, recordkeeping, risk-rating,
    and ongoing anti-money-laundering duties. The precise research question is whether
    Mosaic may adopt or rely on Harbor’s prior verification, and what records or remediation
    Mosaic must retain when the underlying identity documents are unavailable.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor
    verified the users through a vendor that closed in 2024. Mosaic has pass/fail
    results for all users but lacks the underlying documents for users onboarded before
    2023. Mosaic’s compliance team has not confirmed whether its own program permits
    reliance.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program and applicable law permit reliance on Harbor’s
    process and retained results, Mosaic may be able to migrate some users without
    full reverification. Mosaic would still need evidence that the prior process,
    data, sanctions screening, risk rating, and records meet the applicable requirements.\n\nIf
    reliance is not permitted, or if the evidence is inadequate, Mosaic will need
    reverification or another approved remediation. Until then, it should restrict
    the affected accounts or delay their migration. This control does not resolve
    licensing, alert, or monitoring issues.\n\n**Next step**\n\nCompliance should
    document the applicable program rule, divide users into supported and unsupported
    groups, and define the evidence or reverification needed for each group. The result
    must support a clear migration rule for pre-2023 users.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start
    -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38 -->\n### SAR and alert handling:
    obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor's ~40 open alerts and SARs, and
    successor liability\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe approximately 40 open alerts
    and recent SAR history require authorized review before Mosaic accepts the related
    users and activity without restrictions. The current record does not show whether
    the alerts are routine, overdue, linked to material misconduct, or relevant to
    the acquisition terms.\n\nA record gap does not prove a violation. However, unread
    alerts prevent Mosaic from assessing the risk it would take into its platform.\n\n**Rule
    and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. No saved authority establishes
    who must resolve Harbor’s existing alerts, make any required filing, retain related
    records, or perform continuing review after an asset purchase.\n\nThe unverified
    legal premise is that the responsible regulated entity must assess potentially
    suspicious activity and meet applicable reporting and recordkeeping duties. The
    precise research question is how those duties are divided between Harbor and Mosaic
    for pre-close conduct, transferred accounts, and post-close continuing activity.\n\nAccess
    to SAR material can be legally restricted. Diligence must use authorized reviewers
    and approved access controls. This analysis does not direct Harbor to disclose
    or transfer restricted material to an unauthorized person.\n\n**Application**\n\nDiligence
    identified about 40 open alerts and “a handful” of SARs from the last year. None
    have been reviewed for this matter.\n\nOlder conduct may remain Harbor’s responsibility,
    while Mosaic may have duties for activity that continues after migration. The
    asset purchase documents can allocate work and cost between the parties, but contractual
    allocation may not change a regulator’s view of the responsible entity.\n\nIf
    the review finds overdue cases, connected accounts, control failures, or material
    undisclosed conduct, Mosaic may need account restrictions, remediation, revised
    closing protection, or a change to migration scope. If authorized review clears
    the cases and confirms proper handling, this obstacle becomes smaller but does
    not resolve KYC or monitoring continuity.\n\n**Next step**\n\nUse an authorized
    diligence team to triage the alerts and review permitted SAR-related information.
    Produce an aging and risk summary, assign each unresolved case to Harbor or Mosaic,
    and identify any effect on account migration or deal protection.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start
    -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542 -->\n### Monitoring vendor transition:
    continuity of transaction monitoring when the SaaS contract terminates at close\n\n**Current
    answer**\n\nMosaic should validate the replacement transaction-monitoring feed
    before migrated users receive full access. Repointing the feed on day one without
    tested coverage creates a risk that transactions will not be captured, scored,
    or investigated correctly.\n\nIf validation is incomplete, the fallback should
    be continued Harbor coverage, a delayed migration, or transaction restrictions.
    The current record does not show that any fallback is available.\n\n**Rule and
    support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. No saved authority states the
    precise monitoring duty that applies to Harbor or Mosaic.\n\nThe unverified legal
    premise is that the responsible regulated provider must operate monitoring that
    is suitable for its risks and can support alert review and required reporting.
    The precise research question is which monitoring and continuity duties apply
    to each entity at close and during migration.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s third-party
    monitoring contract ends at close. The plan is to repoint Harbor’s transaction
    feed to Mosaic’s engine on day one.\n\nTechnical connectivity alone is not sufficient.
    Validation should establish complete data capture, correct field mapping, suitable
    scenarios and thresholds, timely alert creation, case ownership, historical-data
    availability, reconciliation, and recovery from failed feeds.\n\nThis work depends
    on the operating-provider and KYC decisions. Mosaic’s engine must monitor the
    actual products, customer risks, and funds flow that will exist after close. It
    must also support any continuing review of Harbor’s open cases.\n\n**Next step**\n\nComplete
    an end-to-end test using representative Harbor activity. The result needed to
    proceed is documented data completeness, alert generation, case routing, reconciliation,
    and a tested failure procedure.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start
    -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66 -->\n### Marketing compliance:
    the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money transmission or consumer protection
    implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe bonus should not launch at close+1 until
    its operating terms and disclosures are reviewed. The offer is lower priority
    than licensing, KYC, alerts, and monitoring, but its planned timing leaves little
    room to correct unclear or misleading terms.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue
    has not been researched. No saved authority establishes the rules that apply to
    the proposed promotion.\n\nThe unverified legal premise is that the offer must
    accurately state its eligibility, required transfer, payment timing, limits, exclusions,
    expiration, and any right to reverse the bonus. Its funds flow must also fit the
    approved account and licensing structure. The precise research question is which
    state promotion, consumer-protection, money-transmission, unclaimed-property,
    tax, and disclosure rules apply to the final design.\n\n**Application**\n\nThe
    only reported terms are a $50 bonus on the first transfer and a planned close+1
    launch. The record does not state:\n\n- who qualifies;\n- the minimum or type
    of transfer;\n- who funds the bonus;\n- when it becomes available;\n- whether
    withdrawal or account-duration limits apply;\n- whether the offer is limited by
    state;\n- how disputes, reversals, fraud, and tax reporting are handled; or\n-
    what the customer-facing disclosures will say.\n\nThese terms determine whether
    the campaign is accurate and operationally supportable. The campaign must also
    exclude any state or user group whose migration or service access is held.\n\n**Next
    step**\n\nMarketing should provide the final offer mechanics, customer terms,
    creative material, state scope, and funds flow. Legal and compliance should approve
    that package before launch. If approval is not complete, delay the campaign without
    delaying otherwise lawful migration work.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start
    -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end
    -->\n\n## Alternatives considered\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4
    -->\n### Bank-held funds timing test — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved
    alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
    this test only, a bank would hold the relevant funds while Mosaic controlled transfer
    instructions. The arrangement would depend on contract completion and bank operating
    setup. The test uses a November 15, 2026 migration and December 3, 2026 bank readiness
    date. It also assumes missing pre-2023 identity documents, 40 pending alert cases,
    and monitoring that ends at close.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nBank custody could change
    part of the licensing and safeguarding analysis if the contracts, customer terms,
    control rights, and actual operations support a bank-led model.\n\n**Trade-offs
    and added risks**\n\nOn the test dates, bank integration would be ready 18 days
    after the assumed migration date. The option therefore makes the tested November
    15 launch harder unless readiness moves earlier or migration moves later.\n\nMosaic
    would still control transfer instructions. Bank custody alone does not establish
    that the bank is the regulated service provider or that Mosaic may operate without
    its own authority.\n\n**Issues that remain**\n\nThe option does not resolve missing
    KYC documents, pending alerts, SAR handling, or replacement monitoring. It also
    depends on completed bank contracts and operating setup.\n\n**Next action**\n\nThe
    saved working note names Mara Chen to obtain a dated bank-readiness plan and confirm
    whether the bank can support November 15. This is saved scenario guidance, not
    an assignment or commitment. The note also calls for assigned plans covering identity
    records, alerts, and monitoring.\n\nUse this option only if the bank model is
    legally supportable and can be operational before the chosen migration date. Otherwise,
    use it as a later transition structure rather than a basis for the initial launch.\n\n<!--
    alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6 -->\n### Bank-held funds structure —
    **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
    this hypothetical only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nThe
    model could reduce part of Mosaic’s direct funds-custody role. It could support
    a different licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic performs
    only permitted services.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nCustody alone does
    not resolve who conducts the regulated activity. The option adds dependency on
    bank agreements, consent, account setup, control rights, reconciliation, and operating
    readiness.\n\n**Issues that remain**\n\nThe following points remain open:\n\n-
    who contracts with users;\n- who controls transfer instructions and settlement;\n-
    who records balances and owes repayment;\n- how KYC, monitoring, alerts, SARs,
    privacy, and marketing duties are allocated; and\n- whether each affected state
    accepts the structure.\n\nThe option does not by itself resolve any KYC, alert,
    monitoring, or marketing issue.\n\n**Next action**\n\nPrepare the proposed customer,
    funds, instruction, settlement, ledger, loss, refund, and compliance flows. Compare
    them with the existing full day-one Mosaic model. Use the bank option only if
    those documents and actual operations establish a lawful bank-led structure and
    the bank can be ready on time.\n\n## Next actions\n\n1. **Resolve the state launch
    boundary.**  \n   **Deliverable:** A reconciled license list and state-by-state
    authority matrix.  \n   **Result needed:** Documented authority or an approved
    transition path for every planned post-close activity.  \n   **Dependent activity:**
    Day-one service activation and customer notices.  \n   **Fallback:** Hold regulated
    functions in any state without confirmed authority.  \n   **Proposed owner and
    timing:** Licensing team with state regulatory counsel; start now and finish before
    closing conditions and launch scope are final.\n\n2. **Review the alerts and SAR
    history through authorized channels.**  \n   **Deliverable:** An aging, risk,
    ownership, and remediation summary.  \n   **Result needed:** Each open case has
    an authorized owner, required action, and migration treatment.  \n   **Dependent
    decision:** Which users can migrate without restrictions and whether deal protection
    must change.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict affected accounts and preserve Harbor’s
    handling responsibilities where lawful.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Harbor
    and Mosaic anti-money-laundering leads with deal counsel; complete before migration
    approval.\n\n3. **Set the KYC migration rule.**  \n   **Deliverable:** A documented
    compliance position and user segmentation plan.  \n   **Result needed:** Evidence
    that reliance is permitted and records are sufficient, or a defined reverification
    process.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Migration of pre-2023 users without restrictions.
    \ \n   **Fallback:** Reverify, restrict, or delay the affected accounts.  \n   **Proposed
    owner and timing:** Mosaic compliance; complete before user migration rules and
    notices are final.\n\n4. **Validate transaction monitoring.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
    End-to-end test results and a continuity procedure.  \n   **Result needed:** Complete
    data capture, correct alert generation and routing, reconciliation, and tested
    recovery.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Full post-close transaction access.  \n
    \  **Fallback:** Extend Harbor coverage if available, delay migration, or impose
    transaction limits.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Mosaic anti-money-laundering
    operations and engineering; finish before Harbor’s monitoring contract ends at
    close.\n\n5. **Review the welcome bonus.**  \n   **Deliverable:** Approved mechanics,
    terms, disclosures, state scope, and funds flow.  \n   **Result needed:** An accurate
    and operationally supportable offer that matches launch restrictions.  \n   **Dependent
    activity:** The planned close+1 campaign.  \n   **Fallback:** Delay or narrow
    the campaign.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Marketing with consumer and
    payments counsel; complete after the permitted launch scope is known and before
    campaign release.\n\n## Current work product and supporting records\n\n- [Original
    request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n- [Reported facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n-
    [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
    [Prior dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-dc2adc8aaff5906e6734.md)\n\n[Open
    saved dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-3dc22f6f653187367a96.md)\n\nDossier
    generated and saved."

  - source_id: FILE-000357e0a9c6a0ad233f
    source_label: 'facts.md: # Known Facts


      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~1…'
    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md
    available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks out).

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance and full
      access to Mosaic''s product set.

      - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic Relay
      holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new markets.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic has pass/fail
      results for everyone but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed at Mosaic''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
      launching close+1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.

      - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were already
      KYC''d.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail results
      exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for users onboarded
      before 2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic Relay''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

      - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic buys
      Harbor''s assets)

      - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another institution''s
      prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification required? — Not sure
      / need to check with compliance

      - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the last year?
      — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic Relay
      plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its own? — Use/assume
      Harbor''s licenses

      - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what is the
      plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification and recordkeeping
      obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits
      reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

      - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year been reviewed,
      and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed
      and remain in diligence.

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what is
      the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before onboarding
      those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses
      for the four new markets.


      ## Assumptions


      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and Harbor''s
      MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition without new
      state approval

      - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s
      own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

      - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and validated
      before close without a monitoring gap

      - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state MTL
      regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in 41 states
      (per the request).

      - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
      which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
      (structure not yet confirmed).'
    record_revision: 3a02d2d003cd1a3ad638ac726d9299596bd252c3e3d1d4c3bd3a45b06da29045

    available_excerpt: '# Original Request


      From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      close+1.

      name: request.md
      content: '# Original Request


        From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

        Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


        We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
        plan:


        240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
        One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

        No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

        Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
        opens four new markets.

        Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
        results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded
        before 2023.

        Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
        Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

        Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
        close+1.

        Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs
        from the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


        Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.

        '

  content: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe Harbor Pay migration
    needs legal and compliance review before the planned Nov 15 close. This is the
    accepted working view. It is not a recorded decision.\n\nThis draft recommends
    separating the acquisition close from the launch of regulated services. The asset
    purchase can proceed while Mosaic prepares the migration. Mosaic should not give
    all Harbor users full access on day one unless:\n\n1. Mosaic has documented authority
    for each post-close service in each affected state.\n2. Compliance approves reliance
    on Harbor’s know-your-customer (KYC) results or completes required remediation.\n3.
    Authorized reviewers assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity report
    (SAR) history.\n4. Mosaic tests the replacement transaction-monitoring feed and
    shows that it has no material coverage gap.\n\nIf a condition is not met, Mosaic
    should hold the affected state launch, restrict affected accounts, or delay full
    product access. The planned $50 welcome bonus should wait until its structure,
    terms, funding, and disclosures are reviewed.\n\nNo decision has been recorded.\n\n###
    Assumptions used\n\n- Harbor is subject to applicable state money-transmission
    and federal anti-money-laundering requirements. The licensing, KYC, alert, and
    monitoring answers depend on this unverified legal premise.\n- Mosaic will become
    the operating provider after close. This affects whether Harbor could remain the
    licensed provider during a transition.\n- The analysis does not assume that Harbor’s
    licenses transfer, that its KYC results satisfy Mosaic’s program, or that monitoring
    can continue without a gap.\n- The older assumption that the acquisition structure
    was unknown is superseded. The reported structure is an asset purchase.\n- Mosaic’s
    reported 41-state license footprint is a reported fact, not an assumption.\n\n###
    Record conflicts\n\n- Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has
    licenses in 41 states, and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint
    is three states larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says the
    acquisition opens four new markets. This affects which states require separate
    authority or launch restrictions. The license lists and the intended meaning of
    “market” are needed.\n- Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`. The
    reported close is “Nov 15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake.
    A saved hypothetical uses November 15, 2026, but that does not establish the actual
    closing year. The operative close date and year remain unresolved.\n\n## Decision
    question\n\nDoes any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review
    before the Nov 15 close?\n\n## Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045
    -->\n### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under
    the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive the
    acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic should not treat Harbor’s money transmitter
    licenses as assets that automatically transfer in the reported asset purchase.
    Mosaic should not launch regulated services in a state without documented authority
    for its complete post-close activity.\n\nThe acquisition may close separately
    from the service launch. A state launch hold is the current fallback where authority
    is not established.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nSaved research concludes that the
    answer must be determined state by state. The review must cover Mosaic’s authority,
    transaction notices or approvals, interim operation, outstanding obligations,
    and Harbor’s license surrender.\n\nFour sources were retrieved, but no operative
    passage was selected, read, or verified. They do not establish the governing rule
    in any affected state:\n\n- [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
    [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]\n- [source:SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4]\n- [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]\n-
    [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]\n\nThe model act is not proof of any state’s
    adopted law. The premise that an asset purchase does not automatically give Mosaic
    Harbor’s operating authority remains an unverified state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor
    reportedly has licenses in 38 states. Mosaic reportedly has licenses in 41 states.
    Their combined footprint is reported as 44 states. Mosaic plans to use or assume
    Harbor’s licenses in the new markets.\n\nThe unified Mosaic account, combined
    balance, and access to Mosaic products suggest that Mosaic may become the actual
    provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or licenses active might not authorize
    Mosaic’s conduct.\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider during a transition
    only if customer contracts, funds flow, operating control, licenses, bonds, records,
    and applicable state rules support that result. The written structure must match
    actual operations.\n\nA partner bank holding funds would not by itself resolve
    the issue. The result still depends on who contracts with users, controls transfers,
    owes repayment, records balances, resolves errors, and performs regulated duties.\n\n**Next
    step**\n\nIdentify the Harbor-only jurisdictions and complete a state matrix.
    For each state, determine Mosaic’s authority, required filings or approvals, operation
    while an application is pending, transfer of customer obligations, bank custody
    and control, Harbor’s run-off duties, and the required launch restriction if authority
    is not established.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start
    -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved
    research snapshot. Its facts and assumptions may predate later records. Use the
    current answer above for application to the current matter.\n\nDo not rely on
    transferability without an applicable state rule, approval, or written regulator
    position.\n\nThe answer must be determined state by state and must cover more
    than technical change-of-control rules.\n\nThis path is possible only if Harbor
    remains the real provider and the relevant states permit the arrangement. The
    unified Mosaic account design may conflict with that position.\n\nThe result depends
    on the contracts and actual funds flow. Custody alone should not be treated as
    a licensing exemption or transfer mechanism.\n\nResearch saved. 4 sources retrieved;
    0 with passages read.\n\nNext step: Identify the four Harbor-only states and complete
    one matrix covering license authority, transaction filings, interim operation,
    bank custody, outstanding obligations, and license surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed
    analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical answer**\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money transmitter
    licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.** Use this closing
    rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated launch by Mosaic in that
    state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close. However, Mosaic should not activate
    regulated services in the four Harbor-only states unless one of these conditions
    is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own license.\n2. The state approves a transfer
    or other license change.\n3. The regulator confirms a lawful interim structure.\n4.
    Harbor remains the real licensed provider under a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic
    blocks regulated functions in that state.\n\nThe planned unified Mosaic account
    is important. It suggests that Mosaic, not Harbor, will become the service provider.
    If that is correct, keeping Harbor’s legal entity and licenses alive might not
    give Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No verified operative authority retrieved.**
    The collection found the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act and a
    New York regulator licensing page. However, no exact provision about an asset
    sale, license transfer, interim operation, or custody was available for review.
    Also, a model act is not proof of the law adopted in a specific state. The state-specific
    conclusions below remain conditional.\n\n**Work needed before launch**\n\n| Work
    | Why | Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n|
    Identify the four Harbor-only states | These states have the clearest authority
    gap | Licensing team | Now | Confirmed license list and covered activities | Block
    regulated functions in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every affected state
    | Transfer, notice, approval, and surrender rules can differ | State regulatory
    counsel | Before the closing conditions are final | Applicable rule, filing deadline,
    regulator response, and license status | Delay migration in the affected state
    |\n| Confirm the post-close service provider | The licensed entity must match
    the actual operating model | Product and deal counsel | Before customer notices
    and account design are final | Contracts, user interface, funds-flow diagram,
    and operating roles | Keep Harbor as the actual provider where permitted |\n|
    Review notices and approvals | An asset sale can create separate seller and buyer
    requirements | Licensing team | Before each state deadline | Filing receipts and
    required approvals or non-objections | Make approval a state launch condition
    |\n| Confirm interim operating authority | A pending application should not be
    assumed to permit operation | State regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable
    rule or written regulator confirmation | Keep Harbor customers segregated or restrict
    transactions |\n| Review partner-bank arrangements | Bank custody does not, by
    itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing position | Payments counsel and bank relationship
    owner | Before balances move | Bank agreements, account titles, control rights,
    reconciliation design, and bank consent | Keep funds and obligations in the existing
    structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and surrender plans | Harbor may retain
    duties for balances, claims, records, and reports | Harbor compliance and deal
    counsel | Before surrender or operational shutdown | Regulator-approved plan and
    continued bonds and financial coverage | Keep Harbor licensed and operational
    longer |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo not search only for a rule called
    “license transfer.” Review each state for:\n\n- sale of substantially all assets;\n-
    change of control;\n- change in business plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n-
    assignment of outstanding payment obligations;\n- change in responsible persons,
    locations, or agents;\n- license surrender or termination;\n- customer agreement
    assignment; and\n- movement of stored balances or customer funds.\n\nAn asset
    purchase might fall outside a technical “change of control” rule because Harbor’s
    ownership does not change. That does not resolve the issue. Harbor might still
    need a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might separately need authority before
    it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe state matrix should distinguish:\n\n-
    notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n- approval before customer migration;\n-
    new license required;\n- operation permitted while an application is pending;\n-
    regulator-approved transition available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n**Interim
    operation**\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for a transition period.
    However, the structure must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA supportable
    structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains responsible to
    customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n- Harbor controls the
    regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses, bonds, and financial coverage
    remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding obligations remain covered.\n-
    Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints, and examinations.\n- Required
    records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational role is permitted.\n- The partner
    bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant regulator permits or accepts the
    structure.\n\nThe present plan creates tension with this approach. A single Mosaic
    account, one combined balance, and full access to Mosaic products make it harder
    to show that Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank custody**\n\nA
    partner bank account is not automatically a substitute for a money transmitter
    license. The key questions concern the complete activity and obligation flow.\n\nFor
    each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1. Who receives the customer’s
    instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit or return the funds?\n3.
    In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is it a custodial or “for benefit
    of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6. Who owns the ledger and resolves
    errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer fails?\n8. Which entity owes the customer
    a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license, bond, and permissible investments cover
    the obligation?\n10. Does the bank agreement permit assignment, migration, or
    a change in the program manager?\n11. Is bank consent required before closing
    or migration?\n12. What happens to funds if Harbor, Mosaic, or the bank relationship
    ends?\n\nA bank-led model might provide a different licensing analysis if the
    bank is the actual provider and Mosaic performs only permitted services. A bank
    account that merely holds funds for Mosaic or Harbor is different. The legal documents,
    customer terms, control rights, and actual operations must all support the claimed
    model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n- account segregation;\n- daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls
    and reserve funding;\n- bank setoff rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n-
    continuity if the account is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n- return
    and chargeback duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures; and\n-
    whether any deposit-insurance statement is accurate for the actual account structure.\n\n**Recommended
    closing position**\n\nKeep the acquisition closing separate from the regulated-service
    launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic
    has documented authority. For overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing
    licenses cover the complete post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender
    Harbor’s licenses or release its bonds until the applicable regulators permit
    it and all outstanding obligations have been assigned, completed, or placed into
    an approved run-off structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change the current
    recommendation. It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody is part of
    the licensing analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch
    history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
    retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
    -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with missing
    underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's independent
    CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe present record does not support
    migration of all users without further review. Mosaic has KYC pass/fail results,
    but it lacks underlying documents for users onboarded before 2023. Compliance
    has not confirmed whether Mosaic’s anti-money-laundering and customer identification
    program (CIP) permits reliance on Harbor’s work.\n\nMosaic should restrict or
    re-verify affected users unless compliance documents a permitted reliance method
    and shows that the available records satisfy it.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
    issue has not been researched. The unverified legal premise is that an entity
    subject to federal anti-money-laundering and CIP duties must follow its own applicable
    program and recordkeeping requirements when it begins serving acquired customers.\n\nThe
    precise research question is whether Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s prior identification
    work after an asset purchase, what reliance conditions apply, and which records
    Mosaic must obtain or reproduce.\n\n**Application**\n\nMosaic plans to move 240,000
    consumer users and 12,000 business accounts into its app on day one without re-verification.
    The scale increases the effect of any program or record gap.\n\nA pass/fail result
    may show Harbor reached a conclusion. It does not establish what data Harbor collected,
    how Harbor verified identity, whether the information remains current, or whether
    Mosaic can produce required records.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program permits this form
    of reliance and the retained data meets the applicable requirements, targeted
    remediation may be enough. If it does not, affected users will require re-verification
    or restricted access before Mosaic provides services that require completed identification.\n\n**Next
    step**\n\nCompliance should issue a written decision that identifies the governing
    Mosaic program provisions, the available Harbor data, the missing evidence, and
    the remediation required for each user group. Product access rules must reflect
    that decision before migration.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start
    -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38 -->\n### SAR and alert handling:
    obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor's ~40 open alerts and SARs, and
    successor liability\n\n**Current answer**\n\nAuthorized personnel should review
    the approximately 40 open alerts and the relevant SAR history before full migration.
    Their existence does not prove a violation or successor liability. Their unread
    status prevents Mosaic from assessing reportable activity, affected accounts,
    unresolved investigations, and deal or migration controls.\n\nThe asset-purchase
    structure does not by itself answer which entity must complete Harbor’s pending
    work or retain related records.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not
    been researched. The unverified legal questions are which entity must investigate
    pre-close activity, make any required SAR filing, retain records, and respond
    to later regulator requests after this asset purchase.\n\nSAR information can
    be subject to strict access and confidentiality limits. Diligence should therefore
    use personnel and procedures authorized to access it. A need for review is not
    an instruction to disclose or transfer restricted material outside a permitted
    process.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor has approximately 40 open alerts and “a
    handful” of SARs from the last year. None has been reviewed in diligence.\n\nIf
    the alerts concern customers who will migrate, Mosaic may need account restrictions,
    enhanced review, or another control before giving them full access. If review
    finds unresolved reportable activity or serious program failures, the result could
    affect migration scope, contractual protections, or whether Harbor must complete
    work before close.\n\nIf the alerts are resolved as false positives and the SAR
    history shows no material control problem, a documented handoff may be sufficient.
    That result cannot be assumed from the current record.\n\n**Next step**\n\nUse
    an authorized review team to classify every open alert, identify any required
    pre-close action, and prepare a lawful handoff and retention plan. Escalate material
    findings into the deal and migration decision before affected accounts receive
    full access.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start -->\nInitial
    analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542 -->\n### Monitoring vendor transition:
    continuity of transaction monitoring when the SaaS contract terminates at close\n\n**Current
    answer**\n\nA day-one feed repoint is not enough by itself. Mosaic should validate
    that its engine receives complete, accurate, and timely Harbor transaction and
    customer data before migrated users receive unrestricted access.\n\nIf validation
    is incomplete, Mosaic should extend the existing service where possible, run both
    systems in parallel, or restrict activity until the replacement is shown to work.\n\n**Rule
    and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. The precise unverified legal
    question is what monitoring Mosaic and Harbor must maintain before, during, and
    after the transition under their applicable anti-money-laundering programs.\n\nIndependent
    of the final legal rule, end-to-end testing is a recommended risk control. It
    is not presented as a separately verified legal requirement.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
    monitoring contract ends at close. The plan is to repoint its transaction feed
    to Mosaic’s engine on day one. This creates a single transition point with no
    recorded overlap or completed validation.\n\nTesting must cover all relevant transaction
    types, customer identifiers, timestamps, amounts, status changes, rejected events,
    and alert generation. It must also address transactions that start before close
    and settle afterward.\n\nA successful connection test would not prove complete
    monitoring. Mosaic needs reconciliation and scenario testing that show the source
    data, rules, alerts, investigation workflow, and record retention work together.\n\n**Next
    step**\n\nComplete an end-to-end validation and reconciliation report before full
    access begins. The report should state tested coverage, known gaps, error handling,
    cutover ownership, and the fallback plan. A material unresolved gap should delay
    or restrict the affected activity.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start
    -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66 -->\n### Marketing compliance:
    the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money transmission or consumer protection
    implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe close-plus-one bonus campaign should
    wait for legal review. The record does not explain its eligibility rules, funding,
    payment method, exclusions, expiry, reversal rights, or disclosures.\n\nThe campaign
    should also wait until Mosaic knows which users and states can lawfully receive
    the underlying transfer service.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not
    been researched. The unverified legal question is whether the final offer structure
    triggers state promotional, consumer-protection, money-transmission, unclaimed-property,
    tax, or related disclosure duties.\n\nA $50 payment is not automatically a deposit
    or interest payment. Its legal treatment depends on the actual offer and funds
    flow.\n\n**Application**\n\nMarketing wants to offer $50 on a user’s first transfer
    at close plus one day. The meaning of “first transfer” and the conditions for
    earning or losing the bonus are unknown.\n\nThe offer could mislead users if it
    advertises service in a state where Mosaic cannot yet operate, omits material
    eligibility terms, or gives Mosaic broad discretion not clearly disclosed. It
    could also increase transaction volume during an unvalidated monitoring transition.\n\n**Next
    step**\n\nPrepare the complete offer terms and funds-flow description. Review
    the eligible users, states, qualifying transfer, payment timing, exclusions, reversals,
    expiry, complaint handling, and disclosures. Delay or narrow the campaign if licensing,
    KYC, or monitoring conditions remain unresolved.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start
    -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end
    -->\n\n## Alternatives considered\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4
    -->\n### Bank-held funds timing test — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved
    alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
    this test only, a bank would hold the relevant funds. Mosaic would control transfer
    instructions, subject to completion of the bank contract and operating setup.
    Migration would occur on November 15, 2026, and bank integration would be ready
    on December 3, 2026. Pre-2023 identity documents would remain missing, 40 alert
    cases would remain pending, and monitoring would end at close.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nBank
    custody could provide a different operating structure for the licensing review.
    It could be useful if the bank becomes the actual provider and the contracts,
    customer terms, control rights, and operations support that role.\n\n**Trade-offs
    and added risks**\n\nOn the hypothetical dates, the bank integration is ready
    18 days after migration. It therefore makes the November 15 migration harder unless
    readiness moves earlier or migration moves later.\n\nA new bank contract is not
    itself a disadvantage. The timing problem exists because the benefit depends on
    completing both the contract and operating setup before migration.\n\n**Issues
    that remain**\n\nBank custody does not resolve missing identity evidence, pending
    alerts, or the loss of monitoring at close. It also does not establish that Mosaic
    can use Harbor’s licenses or that Mosaic is outside state licensing rules while
    it controls transfer instructions.\n\n**Next action**\n\nThe saved working note
    proposes that Mara Chen obtain a dated bank-readiness plan and determine whether
    the bank can support November 15. That scenario-only work should also assign resolution
    of the identity, alert, and monitoring gaps.\n\nUse this option only if the bank
    structure is legally supported and operationally ready before the selected migration
    date.\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6 -->\n### Bank-held funds
    structure — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
    this test only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nThe structure
    could change the licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic
    performs only activities that the law and bank agreement permit.\n\n**Trade-offs
    and added risks**\n\nCustody alone does not transfer Harbor’s licenses or establish
    Mosaic’s authority. A structure that names the bank as provider but leaves Mosaic
    in actual control could fail to achieve its intended benefit.\n\n**Issues that
    remain**\n\nThe alternative leaves open who contracts with users, controls transfer
    instructions and settlement, records balances, owes repayment, and handles KYC,
    monitoring, alerts, SARs, privacy, and marketing.\n\nIt does not resolve the current
    KYC evidence, alert-review, or monitoring gaps.\n\n**Next action**\n\nPrepare
    customer-contract and funds-flow diagrams. Compare the legal documents with actual
    operational control. Use this option only if the bank’s role creates a supported
    legal path and does not delay the migration beyond the business objective.\n\n##
    Next actions\n\n1. **Review the open alerts and SAR history.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
    Authorized case review, account-impact list, filing assessment, and handoff plan.
    \ \n   **Result needed:** Material cases are resolved or controlled before affected
    users receive full access.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Migration scope, account
    restrictions, and deal protections.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict affected accounts,
    require Harbor to complete defined work, or delay their migration.  \n   **Proposed
    owner and timing:** Harbor and Mosaic anti-money-laundering leads, with deal counsel,
    before the final migration decision.\n\n2. **Establish state operating authority.**
    \ \n   **Deliverable:** Reconciled license lists and a state matrix for the complete
    post-close product and funds flow.  \n   **Result needed:** Documented authority,
    approval, or a lawful transition path in each launch state.  \n   **Dependent
    activity:** State launch, account migration, customer notices, and Harbor license
    surrender.  \n   **Fallback:** Hold the affected state launch or keep Harbor as
    the actual provider where supported.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Licensing
    team and state regulatory counsel, before closing conditions and customer communications
    are final.\n\n3. **Resolve KYC reliance and missing records.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
    Written compliance decision and user-segment remediation plan.  \n   **Result
    needed:** A supported basis to rely on Harbor’s KYC or completed re-verification
    for affected users.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Full account access and the
    no-reverification plan.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict or re-verify affected users.
    \ \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Mosaic compliance, before migration rules
    are locked.\n\n4. **Validate monitoring continuity.**  \n   **Deliverable:** End-to-end
    test, reconciliation report, and cutover fallback.  \n   **Result needed:** Complete
    and timely data ingestion, alert generation, investigation workflow, and record
    retention.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Unrestricted post-close transactions.
    \ \n   **Fallback:** Extend Harbor’s service, run both systems, or restrict affected
    activity.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Mosaic compliance technology and
    operations, before cutover approval.\n\n5. **Review the $50 bonus.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
    Final offer terms, funds flow, state scope, and disclosure review.  \n   **Result
    needed:** A clear and supportable promotion limited to users and states approved
    for launch.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Close-plus-one marketing campaign.  \n
    \  **Fallback:** Delay or narrow the offer.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:**
    Marketing counsel and compliance, after launch scope is known and before publication.\n\n##
    Current work product and supporting records\n\n- [Known facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n-
    [Original request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n- [Money transmission

    generated and saved."
