  - source_id: FILE-000357e0a9c6a0ad233f
    source_label: 'facts.md: # Known Facts


      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~1…'
    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md
    available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks out).

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance and full
      access to Mosaic''s product set.

      - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic Relay
      holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new markets.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic has pass/fail
      results for everyone but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed at Mosaic''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
      launching close+1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.

      - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were already
      KYC''d.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail results
      exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for users onboarded
      before 2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic Relay''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

      - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic buys
      Harbor''s assets)

      - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another institution''s
      prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification required? — Not sure
      / need to check with compliance

      - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the last year?
      — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic Relay
      plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its own? — Use/assume
      Harbor''s licenses

      - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what is the
      plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification and recordkeeping
      obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits
      reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

      - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year been reviewed,
      and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed
      and remain in diligence.

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what is
      the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before onboarding
      those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses
      for the four new markets.


      ## Assumptions


      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and Harbor''s
      MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition without new
      state approval

      - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s
      own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

      - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and validated
      before close without a monitoring gap

      - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state MTL
      regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in 41 states
      (per the request).

      - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
      which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
      (structure not yet confirmed).'
    record_revision: 3a02d2d003cd1a3ad638ac726d9299596bd252c3e3d1d4c3bd3a45b06da29045

    available_excerpt: '# Original Request


      From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      name: request.md
      content: '# Original Request


        From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

        Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


        We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
        plan:


        240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
        One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

        No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

        Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
        opens four new markets.

        Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
        results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded
        before 2023.

        Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
        Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

        Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
        close+1.

        Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs
        from the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


        Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.

        '

  content: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe Harbor Pay migration
    needs legal and compliance review before the planned Nov 15 close. This is the
    accepted working view. No decision has been recorded.\n\nThis draft recommends
    continuing close preparation but making the day-one service migration conditional.
    Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full access until:\n\n1. Mosaic has documented
    authority for each post-close service in each affected state.\n2. Compliance confirms
    that Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s know-your-customer (KYC) results, or defines
    and completes remediation.\n3. Authorized reviewers assess Harbor’s open alerts
    and suspicious activity report (SAR) history.\n4. Mosaic tests the replacement
    transaction-monitoring feed and finds no material coverage gap.\n\nIf a condition
    is not met, Mosaic should hold the affected state launch, restrict affected accounts,
    or delay full product access. The $50 welcome bonus should also wait for review
    of its structure, terms, funding, and disclosures.\n\nThe saved material does
    not establish that the acquisition close itself must wait. However, the unread
    alerts and SAR history could affect deal terms, risk allocation, or the decision
    to close.\n\n### Assumptions used\n\n- Harbor is subject to the state money-transmission
    and federal anti-money-laundering requirements discussed below. The licensing,
    KYC, alert, and monitoring conclusions depend on this unverified legal premise.\n-
    Mosaic will become the operating provider when Harbor users receive a unified
    Mosaic account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products. The licensing
    analysis depends on this inference.\n- The analysis does not assume that Harbor’s
    licenses transfer, that Harbor’s KYC results satisfy Mosaic’s program, or that
    the monitoring transition will work without a gap.\n\n### Record conflicts\n\n-
    Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states,
    and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states
    larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says the acquisition opens
    four new markets. The license lists and the intended meaning of “market” are needed.
    Until then, the states requiring separate authority cannot be identified reliably.\n-
    Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`. The reported close is “Nov
    15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake. A saved hypothetical uses
    November 15, 2026, but that does not establish the actual closing year. The operative
    close date and year remain unresolved.\n\n## Decision question\n\nDoes any part
    of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before the Nov 15 close?\n\n##
    Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045 -->\n### Money transmission
    licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under the combined 44-state footprint
    and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive the acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic
    should not treat Harbor’s money transmitter licenses as assets that automatically
    move to Mosaic through the reported asset purchase. Mosaic should not start regulated
    services in a state unless it has documented authority for its complete post-close
    activity.\n\nThe acquisition close and the service launch can be managed as separate
    milestones. If authority is not established, the present fallback is to hold the
    affected state launch or restrict regulated functions.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nSaved
    research concludes that the answer must be determined state by state. The review
    must cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction notices or approvals, interim operations,
    outstanding customer obligations, and Harbor’s license surrender.\n\nFour sources
    were retrieved, but no operative passage was selected, read, or verified. They
    do not establish the rule in any affected state:\n\n- [Money transmission research
    packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n- [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]\n-
    [source:SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4]\n- [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]\n- [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]\n\nThe
    model act is not proof of any state’s adopted law. The premise that an asset purchase
    does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority remains an unverified
    state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nMosaic plans to use or assume Harbor’s
    licenses in the new markets. The planned unified Mosaic account, combined balance,
    and access to Mosaic products indicate that Mosaic may become the actual provider.
    If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or licenses active might not authorize Mosaic’s
    conduct.\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider during a transition only
    if customer contracts, funds flow, operating control, licenses, bonds, records,
    and applicable state rules support that result. The documents and actual operations
    must match.\n\nA partner bank holding funds would not alone resolve the issue.
    The analysis still depends on who contracts with users, controls transfers, owes
    repayment, records balances, resolves errors, and performs regulated duties.\n\n**Next
    step**\n\nIdentify the Harbor-only jurisdictions and prepare a state matrix. For
    each state, determine Mosaic’s authority, required filings or approvals, operation
    while an application is pending, treatment of customer obligations, Harbor’s run-off
    duties, and the launch restriction needed if authority is not established.\n\n<!--
    retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved
    research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved research snapshot. Its facts
    and assumptions may predate later records. Use the current answer above for application
    to the current matter.\n\nDo not rely on transferability without an applicable
    state rule, approval, or written regulator position.\n\nThe answer must be determined
    state by state and must cover more than technical change-of-control rules.\n\nThis
    path is possible only if Harbor remains the real provider and the relevant states
    permit the arrangement. The unified Mosaic account design may conflict with that
    position.\n\nThe result depends on the contracts and actual funds flow. Custody
    alone should not be treated as a licensing exemption or transfer mechanism.\n\nResearch
    saved. 4 sources retrieved; 0 with passages read.\n\nNext step: Identify the four
    Harbor-only states and complete one matrix covering license authority, transaction
    filings, interim operation, bank custody, outstanding obligations, and license
    surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical answer**\n\n**Do
    not treat Harbor’s money transmitter licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in
    the asset purchase.** Use this closing rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means
    no regulated launch by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still
    close. However, Mosaic should not activate regulated services in the four Harbor-only
    states unless one of these conditions is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own license.\n2.
    The state approves a transfer or other license change.\n3. The regulator confirms
    a lawful interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains the real licensed provider under
    a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks regulated functions in that state.\n\nThe
    planned unified Mosaic account is important. It suggests that Mosaic, not Harbor,
    will become the service provider. If that is correct, keeping Harbor’s legal entity
    and licenses alive might not give Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No verified
    operative authority retrieved.** The collection found the CSBS Model Money Transmission
    Modernization Act and a New York regulator licensing page. However, no exact provision
    about an asset sale, license transfer, interim operation, or custody was available
    for review. Also, a model act is not proof of the law adopted in a specific state.
    The state-specific conclusions below remain conditional.\n\n**Work needed before
    launch**\n\n| Work | Why | Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence to proceed |
    Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Identify the four Harbor-only states
    | These states have the clearest authority gap | Licensing team | Now | Confirmed
    license list and covered activities | Block regulated functions in those states
    |\n| Build a matrix for every affected state | Transfer, notice, approval, and
    surrender rules can differ | State regulatory counsel | Before the closing conditions
    are final | Applicable rule, filing deadline, regulator response, and license
    status | Delay migration in the affected state |\n| Confirm the post-close service
    provider | The licensed entity must match the actual operating model | Product
    and deal counsel | Before customer notices and account design are final | Contracts,
    user interface, funds-flow diagram, and operating roles | Keep Harbor as the actual
    provider where permitted |\n| Review notices and approvals | An asset sale can
    create separate seller and buyer requirements | Licensing team | Before each state
    deadline | Filing receipts and required approvals or non-objections | Make approval
    a state launch condition |\n| Confirm interim operating authority | A pending
    application should not be assumed to permit operation | State regulatory counsel
    | Before close | Applicable rule or written regulator confirmation | Keep Harbor
    customers segregated or restrict transactions |\n| Review partner-bank arrangements
    | Bank custody does not, by itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing position | Payments
    counsel and bank relationship owner | Before balances move | Bank agreements,
    account titles, control rights, reconciliation design, and bank consent | Keep
    funds and obligations in the existing structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and
    surrender plans | Harbor may retain duties for balances, claims, records, and
    reports | Harbor compliance and deal counsel | Before surrender or operational
    shutdown | Regulator-approved plan and continued bonds and financial coverage
    | Keep Harbor licensed and operational longer |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo
    not search only for a rule called “license transfer.” Review each state for:\n\n-
    sale of substantially all assets;\n- change of control;\n- change in business
    plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n- assignment of outstanding payment obligations;\n-
    change in responsible persons, locations, or agents;\n- license surrender or termination;\n-
    customer agreement assignment; and\n- movement of stored balances or customer
    funds.\n\nAn asset purchase might fall outside a technical “change of control”
    rule because Harbor’s ownership does not change. That does not resolve the issue.
    Harbor might still need a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might separately
    need authority before it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe state matrix should
    distinguish:\n\n- notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n- approval before
    customer migration;\n- new license required;\n- operation permitted while an application
    is pending;\n- regulator-approved transition available; and\n- no supported interim
    path.\n\n**Interim operation**\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for
    a transition period. However, the structure must be real, not only contractual
    language.\n\nA supportable structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor
    remains responsible to customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n-
    Harbor controls the regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses, bonds,
    and financial coverage remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding obligations
    remain covered.\n- Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints, and examinations.\n-
    Required records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational role is permitted.\n-
    The partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant regulator permits or
    accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan creates tension with this approach.
    A single Mosaic account, one combined balance, and full access to Mosaic products
    make it harder to show that Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank
    custody**\n\nA partner bank account is not automatically a substitute for a money
    transmitter license. The key questions concern the complete activity and obligation
    flow.\n\nFor each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1. Who receives
    the customer’s instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit or return
    the funds?\n3. In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is it a custodial or
    “for benefit of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6. Who owns the ledger
    and resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer fails?\n8. Which entity
    owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license, bond, and permissible
    investments cover the obligation?\n10. Does the bank agreement permit assignment,
    migration, or a change in the program manager?\n11. Is bank consent required before
    closing or migration?\n12. What happens to funds if Harbor, Mosaic, or the bank
    relationship ends?\n\nA bank-led model might provide a different licensing analysis
    if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic performs only permitted services.
    A bank account that merely holds funds for Mosaic or Harbor is different. The
    legal documents, customer terms, control rights, and actual operations must all
    support the claimed model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n- account segregation;\n- daily
    reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and reserve funding;\n- bank setoff rights;\n- liens
    and security interests;\n- continuity if the account is frozen;\n- treatment of
    pending transfers;\n- return and chargeback duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n-
    customer disclosures; and\n- whether any deposit-insurance statement is accurate
    for the actual account structure.\n\n**Recommended closing position**\n\nKeep
    the acquisition closing separate from the regulated-service launch.\n\nFor the
    four Harbor-only states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic has documented
    authority. For overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing licenses cover
    the complete post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender Harbor’s
    licenses or release its bonds until the applicable regulators permit it and all
    outstanding obligations have been assigned, completed, or placed into an approved
    run-off structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change the current recommendation.
    It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody is part of the licensing analysis,
    but custody alone does not cure an authority gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch
    history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
    retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
    -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with missing
    underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's independent
    CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe saved material does not support
    a full day-one migration with no re-verification. Mosaic has not confirmed whether
    its anti-money-laundering and customer identification program permits reliance
    on Harbor’s prior KYC. The missing pre-2023 records may prevent Mosaic from showing
    that its own requirements are met.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program permits reliance and
    the retained evidence meets its requirements, targeted remediation may be sufficient.
    If it does not, affected users should be re-verified or restricted before receiving
    relevant services.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched.
    The unverified legal premise is that Mosaic must apply its own risk-based customer
    identification, recordkeeping, and anti-money-laundering controls when it becomes
    the service provider.\n\nThe precise research question is whether Mosaic may rely
    on identification work completed by Harbor, and what evidence, agreement, certification,
    or remediation is required when underlying documents are unavailable.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
    former KYC vendor shut down in 2024. Mosaic has pass/fail results for all users,
    but it lacks underlying documents for users onboarded before 2023. A pass/fail
    result shows that a process produced an outcome. It does not establish which information
    was collected, how identity was verified, whether required records were retained,
    or whether Harbor’s process matches Mosaic’s program.\n\nThe affected population
    is not stated. That count matters because it affects whether remediation can finish
    before launch and whether restrictions can be targeted.\n\n**Next step**\n\nCompliance
    should compare Harbor’s KYC process and available records with Mosaic’s written
    program. The required output is a documented reliance or remediation decision,
    the affected user count, and account controls for users who do not meet the approved
    standard.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start -->\nInitial
    analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38 -->\n### SAR and alert handling:
    obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor's ~40 open alerts and SARs, and
    successor liability\n\n**Current answer**\n\nAuthorized reviewers should assess
    the approximately 40 open alerts and the SAR history before Mosaic accepts unrestricted
    activity from the affected users. The saved facts do not establish that Mosaic
    inherits every Harbor duty, but the unread material could reveal reportable conduct,
    control failures, customer risk, or facts relevant to the acquisition.\n\n**Rule
    and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. The legal treatment may depend
    on which entity identified the conduct, when relevant deadlines began, which entity
    remains responsible after the asset purchase, what the purchase agreement assigns,
    and whether applicable law permits access to specific SAR material.\n\nSAR information
    is sensitive. Diligence must distinguish lawful access by authorized personnel
    from disclosure or transfer of restricted material. The precise research question
    is which entity must review, decide, file, retain, and continue monitoring each
    pre-close and post-close matter.\n\n**Application**\n\nDiligence identified approximately
    40 open alerts and “a handful” of SARs from the last year. None has been reviewed.
    The record does not identify the alert dates, subjects, conduct, status, prior
    decisions, or affected accounts.\n\nThis is more than a record gap. The unread
    material could change account migration controls and the deal’s risk allocation.
    It does not, by itself, prove a violation or successor liability.\n\n**Next step**\n\nUse
    authorized personnel to create a privileged case inventory. Classify each alert
    by age, subject, activity, deadline, disposition, required action, and affected
    account. Separately identify what SAR information Mosaic may lawfully review or
    receive. Escalate any material findings into migration controls and the deal review.\n\n<!--
    retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start -->\nInitial analysis — no
    completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542 -->\n### Monitoring vendor transition:
    continuity of transaction monitoring when the SaaS contract terminates at close\n\n**Current
    answer**\n\nA day-one feed change is not enough by itself. Mosaic should validate
    that its monitoring system receives complete and accurate Harbor data, applies
    suitable rules, produces alerts, and supports investigation without a material
    gap.\n\nIf validation is incomplete, Mosaic should extend the existing service
    if possible, limit migrated activity, or delay full product access.\n\n**Rule
    and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. The conditional premise is
    that, if Mosaic and Harbor are subject to applicable anti-money-laundering duties,
    their monitoring controls must remain effective through the transition. A specific
    legal test and any applicable examination guidance have not been verified.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
    monitoring contract terminates at close. The plan is to point Harbor’s transaction
    feed to Mosaic’s engine on day one. This creates a single transition point with
    no reported overlap period.\n\nThe saved record does not show field mapping, historical-data
    transfer, rule coverage, alert generation, reconciliation, access to old cases,
    failure handling, or test results. The open Harbor alerts also create a dependency:
    a new feed does not resolve existing cases.\n\n**Next step**\n\nComplete an end-to-end
    test before unrestricted launch. The evidence should include data reconciliation,
    rule and scenario coverage, sample alert results, historical access, case ownership,
    failure procedures, and an approved rollback or restriction plan.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start
    -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end
    -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66 -->\n### Marketing compliance:
    the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money transmission or consumer protection
    implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe $50 welcome campaign should not launch
    at close+1 until its structure and disclosures are reviewed. The offer is lower
    priority than licensing, KYC, alerts, and monitoring, but it could create misleading
    claims or operational obligations if customers cannot use the promoted transfer
    service in every advertised state.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not
    been researched. The applicable analysis may depend on consumer-protection rules,
    state promotional requirements, the funds flow, and the terms governing the bonus.
    No saved authority establishes that the bonus is a deposit, interest payment,
    or regulated transfer product.\n\nThe precise research question is whether the
    final offer structure requires specific terms, disclosures, eligibility limits,
    licensing coverage, or treatment of the bonus funds.\n\n**Application**\n\nThe
    only settled details are a $50 bonus on the first transfer and a proposed launch
    at close+1. The record does not state who funds the bonus, which users qualify,
    the required transfer amount, payment timing, expiration, exclusions, reversal
    rights, tax treatment, or how restrictions will be disclosed.\n\nThe campaign
    also depends on the other workstreams. Mosaic should not advertise immediate access
    in a state or to a user group whose migration remains restricted.\n\n**Next step**\n\nMarketing
    should provide the final offer terms, user journey, target jurisdictions, funding
    flow, and draft claims. Legal review should then confirm that the disclosures
    match actual eligibility, service availability, payment timing, and account restrictions.\n\n<!--
    retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start -->\nInitial analysis — no
    completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end
    -->\n\n## Alternatives considered\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4
    -->\n### Bank-held funds timing test — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved
    alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
    this test only, a bank holds the relevant funds while Mosaic controls transfer
    instructions. The model depends on completion of the bank contract and operating
    setup. It assumes migration on November 15, 2026, and bank readiness on December
    3, 2026. It also assumes missing pre-2023 identity documents, 40 pending alerts,
    and monitoring ending at close.\n\n**Effect on the objective**\n\nThe option may
    change the funds-custody analysis. It does not establish that Mosaic can perform
    the regulated activity without its own authority.\n\nOn the hypothetical dates,
    it makes a November 15 migration harder because bank readiness is December 3,
    18 days later.\n\n**Added risks**\n\nThe option adds contract and integration
    dependencies. If the bank cannot complete its agreement and setup by migration,
    the structure is not operational.\n\n**Issues left unresolved**\n\nBank custody
    does not resolve missing identity records, pending alerts, SAR handling, or the
    monitoring transition. It also does not answer who contracts with users, controls
    transfers, owes repayment, and performs regulated duties.\n\n**Next action**\n\nThe
    saved working note proposes that Mara Chen obtain a dated bank-readiness plan
    and confirm whether the bank can support November 15. This is part of the hypothetical
    note, not a recorded assignment or decision. Use this option only if the bank
    structure is legally supportable and ready before the actual migration date.\n\n<!--
    alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6 -->\n### Bank-held funds structure —
    **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
    this test only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Effect on the objective**\n\nA
    bank-held model could support a different licensing analysis if the bank is the
    actual provider and Mosaic performs only permitted services. Mere custody does
    not establish that result.\n\n**Added risks**\n\nThe structure requires clear
    contracts, control rights, bank consent, funds-flow design, customer terms, reconciliation,
    and operating responsibility. It could add implementation time without solving
    the launch conditions.\n\n**Issues left unresolved**\n\nThe alternative leaves
    open who contracts with users, controls transfer instructions and settlement,
    records balances, owes repayment, and handles KYC, monitoring, alerts, SARs, privacy,
    and marketing. It does not resolve those issues merely by moving the funds.\n\n**Next
    action**\n\nPrepare the proposed contracts, customer terms, funds-flow diagram,
    and operating roles. Compare them with the state licensing matrix. Use this structure
    only where the documents, actual operations, bank approval, and applicable state
    rules support it.\n\n## Next actions\n\n1. **Licensing authority matrix.**  \n
    \  **Proposed owner:** State regulatory counsel with the licensing team.  \n   **Timing:**
    Before closing conditions, customer notices, and account design are final.  \n
    \  **Result needed:** A verified list of affected states and documented authority,
    filing requirements, interim options, and launch restrictions.  \n   **Dependent
    activity:** State-by-state migration and access to Mosaic products.  \n   **Fallback:**
    Hold regulated functions in any state without documented authority.\n\n2. **Alert
    and SAR diligence review.**  \n   **Proposed owner:** Authorized anti-money-laundering
    compliance reviewers with deal counsel.  \n   **Timing:** Before the close decision
    and before affected accounts receive unrestricted access.  \n   **Result needed:**
    A case inventory, required actions, lawful information-access plan, and identification
    of any deal or migration impact.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Deal risk allocation
    and account migration.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict affected accounts and preserve
    Harbor’s case-handling capacity while issues remain open.\n\n3. **KYC reliance
    and remediation decision.**  \n   **Proposed owner:** Mosaic compliance.  \n   **Timing:**
    Before migrated users receive full product access.  \n   **Result needed:** Written
    confirmation that reliance is permitted and adequately supported, or a remediation
    plan with the affected user count.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Migration without
    re-verification.  \n   **Fallback:** Re-verify or restrict users who do not meet
    the approved standard.\n\n4. **Monitoring transition validation.**  \n   **Proposed
    owner:** Mosaic compliance and monitoring operations.  \n   **Timing:** Before
    Harbor’s monitoring service ends or migrated transactions begin.  \n   **Result
    needed:** Successful end-to-end testing, reconciliation, historical access, case
    ownership, and rollback controls.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Unrestricted transaction
    activity after close.  \n   **Fallback:** Extend the existing service if possible,
    restrict activity, or delay full access.\n\n5. **Welcome bonus review.**  \n   **Proposed
    owner:** Marketing counsel with product and compliance teams.  \n   **Timing:**
    Before campaign approval and after launch restrictions are known.  \n   **Result
    needed:** Final terms and disclosures that match the actual funds flow, eligibility,
    state availability, and payment process.  \n   **Dependent activity:** The planned
    close+1 campaign.  \n   **Fallback:** Delay or narrow the campaign.\n\n## Current
    work product and supporting records\n\n- [Known facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n-
    [Original request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n- [Money transmission
    research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
    [Completed intake work item](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/work-items/WI-20260909-dc797b.md)\n-
    [Prior dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-e1dcd612539ad45c6d6f.md)\n\n[Open
    saved dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-eecf5c02c431c10638ea.md)\n\nDossier
    generated and saved."

  - source_id: FILE-000357e0a9c6a0ad233f
    source_label: 'facts.md: # Known Facts


      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~1…'
    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md
    available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks out).

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance and full
      access to Mosaic''s product set.

      - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic Relay
      holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new markets.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic has pass/fail
      results for everyone but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed at Mosaic''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
      launching close+1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.

      - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were already
      KYC''d.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail results
      exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for users onboarded
      before 2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic Relay''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

      - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic buys
      Harbor''s assets)

      - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another institution''s
      prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification required? — Not sure
      / need to check with compliance

      - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the last year?
      — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic Relay
      plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its own? — Use/assume
      Harbor''s licenses

      - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what is the
      plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification and recordkeeping
      obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits
      reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

      - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year been reviewed,
      and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed
      and remain in diligence.

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what is
      the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before onboarding
      those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses
      for the four new markets.


      ## Assumptions


      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and Harbor''s
      MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition without new
      state approval

      - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s
      own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

      - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and validated
      before close without a monitoring gap

      - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state MTL
      regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in 41 states
      (per the request).

      - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
      which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
      (structure not yet confirmed).'

        working_ask: Does the Harbor Pay acquisition migration require legal review
          before the Nov 15 close, and what legal workstreams must be addressed pre-close
          (money transmission licensing, KYC/BSA-AML, SAR/alerts handling, monitoring
          vendor transition, and the welcome bonus campaign)?
        issues:
        - 'Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under the
          combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer/survive
          the acquisition'
        - 'BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with missing underlying
          documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay''s independent CIP/AML
          obligations'
        - 'SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor''s
          ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability'
        - 'Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring when
          the SaaS contract terminates at close'
        - 'Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money transmission
          or consumer protection implications'

        - Acquisition structure (asset vs. stock purchase) — determines whether Harbor's
          MTLs and regulatory obligations transfer to Mosaic Relay
        - Whether Harbor's state MTLs can be assumed/transferred or must be re-applied

        - Whether Mosaic Relay's own AML program and CIP can lawfully rely on Harbor's
          prior KYC without re-verification
        - Details of the ~40 open alerts and SARs (nature, age, whether any are unresolved
          or reportable)
        - Whether the $50 welcome bonus is a deposit/interest-like offer implicating
          state money transmission or consumer protection rules

        - State money transmitter license transfer/assumption requirements in an acquisition
          context
        - BSA/AML CIP obligations when relying on a prior financial institution's
          KYC in a merger/acquisition
        - Successor obligations for open SARs and alerts in an acquisition

      From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
      close+1.

      the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.

      name: request.md
      content: '# Original Request


        From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

        Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


        We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
        plan:


        240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
        One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

        No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

        Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
        opens four new markets.

        Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
        results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded
        before 2023.

        Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
        Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

        Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
        close+1.

        Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs
        from the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


        Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.

        '

- message_id: MSG-20260912-45f21e

  role: assistant
  content: '## Harbor 2 — preparation note (close targeted Nov 15)


    **Controlling question:** does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration
    need legal review before the Nov 15 close? The newest turn ("Generate the Dossier")
    and the surrounding bank-held-funds comparisons are supporting work; they do not
    change that question. The record contains **no recorded decisions** at all, all
    five registered issues are `open`, and one intake question — how the $50 bonus
    is structured — was left open with no answer.


    **Lawyer reframe.** Dana''s framing is "it''s really just a data migration." The
    reframe is that the migration *is* the regulated event: on day 1 Mosaic Relay
    onboards 252,000 accounts into its own licensed product set with no re-verification,
    repoints monitoring, and launches a cash offer — under an asset-purchase structure
    in which nothing about Harbor''s licenses or compliance record transfers by default.
    The operative question is therefore not "can we inherit Harbor''s status," but
    **"what must Mosaic obtain, file, decide or preserve in its own name before Nov
    15, and which parts of the stated deal upside are not actually available at close."**


    **Three premises the record lets us test**


    1. *"Just a data migration."* Fails. The day-1 cutover is the moment CIP, licensing,
    monitoring and disclosure obligations attach to 252k accounts.

    2. *"44 states is a nice win — opens four new markets."* Fails on the arithmetic
    and on the law. Harbor 38 + Mosaic 41 with a 44-state union yields **three** new
    states, not four, and the states are never named; and the plan to "use/assume"
    Harbor''s licenses rests on an assumption the record still marks open ([source:ASM-20260909-29b823]),
    against the saved position that transferability should not be relied on without
    a state rule, approval or written regulator position.

    3. *"No re-verification — they were already KYC''d."* Unresolved. Whether Mosaic''s
    own AML/CIP program permits reliance is unknown, and the pre-2023 records cannot
    be recovered (vendor shut down in 2024; only pass/fail survives).


    **Different route the evidence supports.** Run the remaining ~9 weeks as a *gated
    launch*, not a documentation exercise: read and preserve the alert/SAR backlog;
    decide KYC reliance per cohort and schedule remediation; prove or drop the Harbor-only
    states; validate the monitoring cutover with a parallel run; paper notice/consent,
    new customer terms and closing conditions. If a gate fails, migrate only in the
    overlapping states on day 1 and onboard KYC-deficient accounts with limits — a
    scoped migration rather than the full one.


    **Material issues.** Five registered: money transmission licensing (44-state footprint);
    BSA/AML and KYC reliance for pre-2023 users; SAR and alert handling (~40 open
    alerts, unreviewed); monitoring vendor transition at close; $50 welcome bonus.
    Three that are missing and material: **migration data handling and customer notice**
    (the piece the request actually calls "just a data migration," never analyzed);
    **pre-close papering** (closing conditions, interim operation, allocation of the
    alert/SAR and KYC-record risk — no draft or terms appear anywhere); and **post-close
    access to Harbor''s alert/case history** (the records live in the SaaS system
    whose contract ends at close).


    **Three business priorities** — ranked by effect on the business question, time-fixedness
    and irreversibility, not by difficulty:


    1. **Read and preserve the alert/SAR backlog before anything else is scheduled.**
    It is the only item that can change the deal itself; it is entirely unread, so
    no one can yet say whether a filing is late or an account must be excluded; and
    the records needed to answer it may become inaccessible at close.

    2. **Decide KYC reliance for the pre-2023 cohort — rely, re-verify, or restrict
    access.** It determines whether "no re-verification" is available at all for the
    largest population; the underlying documents cannot be recreated; and re-verifying
    or limiting a cohort is a multi-week program that has to be decided before close,
    not after.

    3. **Prove the Harbor-only states can be served at close, or pull them from day-1
    scope.** It tests the premise the deal is being sold on, state timelines are the
    longest external dependency and cannot be compressed, and serving a state without
    authority is a violation later paperwork cannot undo.


    **Research these first:** the SAR/alert backlog ([source:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38]),
    KYC reliance ([source:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045]), and the licensing position
    for the Harbor-only states ([source:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045]) — in that
    order. If the team needs the earliest single go/no-go decision, licensing converts
    fastest — but it should still follow the backlog read, because a live SAR problem
    can outrank market access.


    **Watch-outs.** The bank-held-funds structure is a saved hypothetical and was
    never adopted; later turns ran under that scenario path, and some prior dossier
    drafts carry scenario scope, so their conclusions are not findings about this
    acquisition. The licensing research has **no citable support** (4 sources retrieved,
    0 passages read; one output headed "No external authority retrieved"), and repeated
    "research queued/running" messages are status, not results. Assumption [source:ASM-20260909-57e86b]
    still calls the structure unconfirmed although the asset purchase is recorded
    and was reconfirmed twice by the user. The matter''s `target_date` field (2026-09-11)
    sits oddly against activity through 2026-09-12 — treat it as unverified. Urgent
    below marks the five items where the close date itself fixes the deadline and
    a mistake cannot be cured afterwards; it is not the same as the top-three ranking.


    *Not performed: no web research. Full-text reads covered the request, facts register,
    intake answers and early analysis; the licensing packet was reviewed at excerpt
    level and prior dossiers treated as fallible synthesis.*


    Dossier research is ready for your choices. No research has started.'

- message_id: MSG-20260912-bb4e32
  action_actor: null
  role: assistant
  content: '## Preparation note


    **Answer:** Yes. Legal and compliance review is required before the November 15,
    2026 close.


    **Lawyer reframe:** The main question is which findings must become conditions
    to close, migrate customers, or launch in a state.


    The planned 44-state launch is not yet supported. Mosaic should prepare a phased
    launch that excludes the four Harbor-only states unless authority is confirmed.
    The bank-held funds option remains hypothetical. The record does not show that
    it will be ready sooner or solve the other compliance gaps.


    ### Material issues


    - Authority to operate in the four Harbor-only states after an asset purchase.

    - Use of Harbor’s prior identity checks when source documents are missing.

    - Review and ownership of about 40 open alerts and prior suspicious activity reports.

    - Continuous transaction monitoring when Harbor’s vendor contract ends.

    - Rights to transfer customer contracts, accounts, balances, and personal data.

    - Legal terms and disclosures for the $50 welcome offer.


    ### Three suggested business priorities


    1. **Confirm the lawful launch area.** Licensing results may require a smaller
    launch or regulator action.

    2. **Make financial-crime controls a migration gate.** Open alerts, missing identity
    records, and monitoring continuity affect the full customer population.

    3. **Protect the customer transfer.** Confirm transfer rights before migration.
    Hold the bonus campaign until the launch area and customer terms are final.


    ### First three issues to research


    1. **Money transmission licensing.** This controls whether Mosaic can launch in
    the four additional states.

    2. **Open alerts and suspicious activity reports.** Existing cases can involve
    time-sensitive duties and irreversible filing or account decisions.

    3. **Monitoring continuity.** Harbor’s current contract ends at close, so a control
    gap could start immediately.


    > A requested saved-record read was unavailable. The writer used the material
    available.


    Dossier research is ready for your choices. No research has started.'

      preparation: '## Preparation note


        **Answer:** Yes. Legal and compliance review is required before the November
        15, 2026 close.


        **Lawyer reframe:** The main question is which findings must become conditions
        to close, migrate customers, or launch in a state.


        The planned 44-state launch is not yet supported. Mosaic should prepare a
        phased launch that excludes the four Harbor-only states unless authority is
        confirmed. The bank-held funds option remains hypothetical. The record does
        not show that it will be ready sooner or solve the other compliance gaps.


        ### Material issues


        - Authority to operate in the four Harbor-only states after an asset purchase.

        - Use of Harbor’s prior identity checks when source documents are missing.

        - Review and ownership of about 40 open alerts and prior suspicious activity
        reports.

        - Continuous transaction monitoring when Harbor’s vendor contract ends.

        - Rights to transfer customer contracts, accounts, balances, and personal
        data.

        - Legal terms and disclosures for the $50 welcome offer.


        ### Three suggested business priorities


        1. **Confirm the lawful launch area.** Licensing results may require a smaller
        launch or regulator action.

        2. **Make financial-crime controls a migration gate.** Open alerts, missing
        identity records, and monitoring continuity affect the full customer population.

        3. **Protect the customer transfer.** Confirm transfer rights before migration.
        Hold the bonus campaign until the launch area and customer terms are final.


        ### First three issues to research


        1. **Money transmission licensing.** This controls whether Mosaic can launch
        in the four additional states.

        2. **Open alerts and suspicious activity reports.** Existing cases can involve
        time-sensitive duties and irreversible filing or account decisions.

        3. **Monitoring continuity.** Harbor’s current contract ends at close, so
        a control gap could start immediately.




        > A requested saved-record read was unavailable. The writer used the material
        available.

        '

      text: "14 \n \nARTICLE V \nMoney Transmission Licenses \nSection 5.01 License
        Required. \n(a) \nA person may not engage in the business of money transmission
        or \nadvertise, solicit, or hold itself out as providing money transmission
        unless the person is licensed \nunder this [Act]; \n(b) \n[Section 5.01(a)]
        does not apply to: \n(1) \nA person that is an authorized delegate of a person
        licensed under \nthis [Act] acting within the scope of authority conferred
        by a written contract with the \nlicensee; or \n(2) \nA person that is exempt
        pursuant to [Section 3.01] and does not \nengage in money transmission outside
        the scope of such exemption. \n(c) \nA license issued under [Section 5.05]
        is not transferable or assignable. \nSection 5.02 Consistent State Licensing.
        \n(a) \nTo establish consistent licensing between [this state] and other states,
        the \n[Commissioner] is authorized and encouraged to: \n(1) \nimplement all
        licensing provisions of this [Act] in a manner that is \nconsistent with other
        states that have adopted this [Act]or multistate licensing processes; \nand
        \n(2) \nparticipate in nationwide protocols for licensing cooperation and
        \ncoordination among state regulators provided that such protocols are consistent
        with this \n[Act]. \n(b) \nIn order to fulfill the purposes of this [Act],
        the [Commissioner] is \nauthorized and encouraged to establish relationships
        or contracts with NMLS or other entities \ndesignated by NMLS to enable the
        [Commissioner] to: \n(1) \ncollect and maintain records; \n(2) \ncoordinate
        multistate licensing processes and supervision processes; \n(3) \nprocess
        fees; and \n(4) \nfacilitate communication between [state] and licensees or
        other \npersons subject to this [Act]. \n(c) \nThe [Commissioner] is authorized
        and encouraged to utilize NMLS for all \naspects of licensing in accordance
        with this [Act], including but not limited to, license applications, \napplications
        for acquisitions of control, surety bonds, reporting, criminal history background\n"

      text: "21 \n \nin a medium prescribed by the [Commissioner]. The renewal report
        must state or contain a \ndescription of each material change in information
        submitted by the licensee in its original license \napplication which has
        not been reported to the [Commissioner]. \n(c) \nThe [Commissioner] for good
        cause may grant an extension of the renewal \ndate. \n(d) \nThe [Commissioner]
        is authorized and encouraged to utilize NMLS to \nprocess license renewals
        provided that such functionality is consistent with this [Section 5.06]. \nSection
        5.07 Maintenance of License. \n(a) \nIf a licensee does not continue to meet
        the qualifications or satisfy the \nrequirements that apply to an applicant
        for a new money transmission license, the [Commissioner] \nmay suspend or
        revoke the licensee's license in accordance with the procedures established
        by this \n[Act] or other applicable state law for such suspension or revocation.
        \n(b) \nAn applicant for a money transmission license must demonstrate that
        it \nmeets or will meet, and a money transmission licensee must at all times
        meet, the requirements in \n[Sections 10.01, 10.02, and 10.03] of this [Act].
        \nARTICLE VI \nAcquisition of Control and Change of Key Individual \nSection
        6.01 Acquisition of Control. \n(a) \nAny person, or group of persons acting
        in concert, seeking to acquire control \nof a licensee shall obtain the written
        approval of the [Commissioner] prior to acquiring control. \nAn individual
        is not deemed to acquire control of a licensee and is not subject to these
        acquisition \nof control provisions when that individual becomes a key individual
        in the ordinary course of \nbusiness. \n(b) \nA person, or group of persons
        acting in concert, seeking to acquire control \nof a licensee shall, in cooperation
        with the licensee: \n(1) \nSubmit an application in a form and in a medium
        prescribed by the \n[Commissioner]; and \n(2) \nSubmit a nonrefundable fee
        of [$X] with the request for approval. \n(c) \nUpon request, the [Commissioner]
        may permit a licensee or the person, or \ngroup of persons acting in concert,
        to submit some or all information required by the \n[Commissioner] pursuant
        to [Section 6.01(b)(1)] without using NMLS. \n(d) \nThe application required
        by [Section 6.01(b)(1)] shall include information \nrequired by [Section 5.04]
        for any new key individuals that have not previously completed the \nrequirements
        of [Section 5.04] for a licensee.\n"

      a new money transmission license, the [Commissioner] \nmay suspend or revoke
      the licensee's license in accordance with the procedures established by this
      \n[Act] or other applicable state law for such suspension or revocation. \n(b)
      \nAn applicant for a money transmission license must demonstrate that it \nmeets
      or will meet, and a money transmission licensee must at all times meet, the
      requirements in \n[Sections 10.01, 10.02, and 10.03] of this [Act]. \nARTICLE
      VI \nAcquisition of Control and Change of Key Individual \nSection 6.01 Acquisition
      of Control. \n(a) \nAny person, or group of persons acting in concert, seeking
      to acquire control \nof a licensee shall obtain the written approval of the
      [Commissioner] prior to acquiring control. \nAn individual is not deemed to
      acquire control of a licensee and is not subject to these acquisition \nof control
      provisions when that individual becomes a key individual in the ordinary course
      of \nbusiness. \n(b) \nA person, or group of persons acting in concert, seeking
      to acquire control \nof a licensee shall, in cooperation with the licensee:
      \n(1) \nSubmit an application in a form and in a medium prescribed by the \n[Commissioner];
      and \n(2) \nSubmit a nonrefundable fee of [$X] with the request for approval.
      \n(c) \nUpon request, the [Commissioner] may permit a licensee or the person,
      or \ngroup of persons acting in concert, to submit some or all information required
      by the \n[Commissioner] pursuant to [Section 6.01(b)(1)] without using NMLS.
      \n(d) \nThe application required by [Section 6.01(b)(1)] shall include information
      \nrequired by [Section 5.04] for any new key individuals that have not previously
      completed the \nrequirements of [Section 5.04] for a licensee.\n"
  - source_id: SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538
    source_version: dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a
    title: '[PDF] CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act'
    extraction_state: complete
    selected_passages:
    - unit_id: p000022
      start: 0
      end: 2612
      page_number: 22
      section_label: null
      body_hash: 175b57e812c71a8532569030d2db7113b5adc94e61bd9922dc0fee5d833c2748
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000022.md
      text: "22 \n \n(e) \nWhen an application for acquisition of control under this
        [Section 6.01] \nappears to include all the items and address all of the matters
        that are required, the application shall \nbe considered complete and the
        [Commissioner] shall promptly notify the applicant in a record of \nthe date
        on which the application was determined to be complete and:15 \n \n(1) \nThe
        [Commissioner] shall approve or deny the application within 60 \ndays after
        the completion date; or \n(2) \nif the application is not approved or denied
        within 60 days after the \ncompletion date: \n(A) \nthe application is approved;
        and \n(B) \nthe person, or group of persons acting in concert, are not \nprohibited
        from acquiring control. \n(3) \nThe [Commissioner] may for good cause extend
        the application \nperiod. \n(f) \nA determination by the [Commissioner] that
        an application is complete and \nis accepted for processing means only that
        the application, on its face, appears to include all of the \nitems and address
        all of the matters that are required, and is not an assessment of the substance
        of \nthe application or of the sufficiency of the information provided. \n(g)
        \nWhen an application is filed and considered complete under [Section \n6.01(e)],
        the [Commissioner] shall investigate the financial condition and responsibility,
        financial \nand business experience, character, and general fitness of the
        person, or group of persons acting in \nconcert, seeking to acquire control.
        The [Commissioner] shall approve an acquisition of control \npursuant to this
        [Section 6.01] if the [Commissioner] finds that all of the following conditions
        have \nbeen fulfilled: \n(1) \nThe requirements of subsections (b) and (d)
        have been met, as \napplicable; and \n(2) \nthe financial condition and responsibility,
        financial and business \nexperience, competence, character, and general fitness
        of the person, or group of persons \nacting in concert, seeking to acquire
        control; and the competence, experience, character, \nand general fitness
        of the key individuals and persons that would be in control of the \nlicensee
        after the acquisition of control indicate that it is in the interest of the
        public to \npermit the person, or group of persons acting in concert, to control
        the licensee. \n(h) \nIf an applicant avails itself or is otherwise subject
        to a multistate licensing \n \n15 Commentary: NMLS will accommodate and streamline
        the process of communicating when applications are \nreceived and when states
        consider them to have been complete. The intent of this Act is for the application
        period to \nbegin on the day an application is determined to be complete.\n"

  - source_id: SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538
    source_version: dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a
    title: '[PDF] CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act'
    extraction_state: complete
    selected_passages:
    - unit_id: p000023
      start: 0
      end: 2523
      page_number: 23
      section_label: null
      body_hash: 83a664c778fbc9de0b4d13270e2a918f6488b461db1a6617e3d36032163068ca
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000023.md
      text: "23 \n \nprocess: \n(1) \nthe [Commissioner] is authorized and encouraged
        to accept the \ninvestigation results of a lead investigative state for the
        purpose of [Section 6.01(g)] if the \nlead investigative state has sufficient
        staffing, expertise, and minimum standards; or \n(2) \nif [state] is a lead
        investigative state, the [Commissioner] is \nauthorized and encouraged to
        investigate the applicant pursuant to [Section 6.01(g)] and \nthe timeframes
        established by agreement through the multistate licensing process. \n(i) \nThe
        [Commissioner] shall issue a formal written notice of the denial of an \napplication
        to acquire control within thirty (30) days of the decision to deny the application.
        The \n[Commissioner] shall set forth in the notice of denial the specific
        reasons for the denial of the \napplication. An applicant whose application
        is denied by the [Commissioner] under this [Section \n6.01(i)] may appeal
        within thirty (30) days16 after receipt of the written notice of the denial
        \n[pursuant to state administrative law procedures]. \n(j) \nThe requirements
        of [Section 6.01(a) and (b)] do not apply to any of the \nfollowing: \n(1)
        \nA person that acts as a proxy for the sole purpose of voting at a \ndesignated
        meeting of the shareholders or holders of voting shares or voting interests
        of a \nlicensee or a person in control of a licensee; \n(2) \nA person that
        acquires control of a licensee by devise or descent; \n(3) \nA person that
        acquires control of a licensee as a personal \nrepresentative, custodian,
        guardian, conservator, or trustee, or as an officer appointed by a \ncourt
        of competent jurisdiction or by operation of law; \n(4) \nA person that is
        exempt under [Section 3.01(g)]; \n(5) \nA person that the [Commissioner] determines
        is not subject to \n[Section 6.01(a)] based on the public interest; \n(6)
        \nA public offering of securities of a licensee or a person in control of
        \na licensee; or \n(7) \nAn internal reorganization of a person in control
        of the licensee \nwhere the ultimate person in control of the licensee remains
        the same. \n(k) \nPersons in [Sections 6.01(j)(2), (3), (4), (6), (7)] in
        cooperation with the \nlicensee shall notify the [Commissioner] within [15]
        days after the acquisition of control.17 \n \n16 Commentary: Administrative
        procedures for challenging a departmental decision may be derived from other
        \naspects of state law. In such a case, this Act should be adjusted to reflect
        the relevant administrative process. \n17 Commentary: Notice is satisfied
        upon updating the licensee’s NMLS record.\n"

      section_label: null
      body_hash: 4732d9c2b053975a4d3cb27db8e99faa4baf45f71eb350fa519e31b5890ac680
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000024.md
      text: "24 \n \n(l) \nStreamlined Acquisition of Control \n(1) \nThe requirements
        of [Section 6.01(a) and (b)] do not apply to a \nperson that has complied
        with and received approval to engage in money transmission \nunder this [Act]
        or was identified as a person in control in a prior application filed with
        and \napproved by the [Commissioner] or by an MSB accredited state pursuant
        to a multistate \nlicensing process, provided that: \n(A) \nthe person has
        not had a license revoked or suspended or \ncontrolled a licensee that has
        had a license revoked or suspended while the person \nwas in control of the
        licensee in the previous 5-years; \n(B) \nif the person is a licensee, the
        person is well managed and \nhas received at least a satisfactory rating for
        compliance at its most recent \nexamination by an MSB accredited state if
        such rating was given; \n(C) \nthe licensee to be acquired is projected to
        meet the \nrequirements of [Sections 10.01, 10.02, and 10.03] of this [Act]
        after the acquisition \nof control is completed, and if the person acquiring
        control is a licensee, that \nlicensee is also projected to meet the requirements
        of [Sections 10.01, 10.02, and \n10.03] of this [Act] after the acquisition
        of control is completed; \n(D) \nthe licensee to be acquired will not implement
        any material \nchanges to its business plan as a result of the acquisition
        of control, and if the person \nacquiring control is a licensee, that licensee
        also will not implement any material \nchanges to its business plan as a result
        of the acquisition of control;  and \n(E) \nthe person provides notice of
        the acquisition in cooperation \nwith the licensee and attests to [Section
        6.01(l)(1)(A), (B), (C), and (D)] in a form \nand in a medium prescribed by
        the [Commissioner]. \n(2) \nIf the notice is not disapproved within 30 days
        after the date on \nwhich the notice was determined to be complete, the notice
        is deemed approved. \n(m) \nBefore filing an application for approval to acquire
        control of a licensee a \nperson may request in writing a determination from
        the [Commissioner] as to whether the person \nwould be considered a person
        in control of a licensee upon consummation of a proposed \ntransaction. If
        the [Commissioner] determines that the person would not be a person in control
        of \na licensee, the proposed Person and transaction is not subject to the
        requirements of [Section \n6.01(a) and (b)] of this [Act]. \n(n) \nIf a multistate
        licensing process includes a determination pursuant to \n[Section 6.01(m)]
        and an applicant avails itself or is otherwise subject to the multistate licensing
        \nprocess: \n(1) \nThe [Commissioner] is authorized and encouraged to accept
        the \ncontrol determination of a lead investigative state with sufficient
        staffing, expertise, and \nminimum standards for the purpose of [Section 6.01(m)];
        or\n"

      body_hash: 2245b178c49fc1f157bf15c133c59f8fcfe9abdf43f0bf94df397229a7889584
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000004.md
      text: "ly for goods or services provided by the issuer or its affiliate or franchisees
        of the issuer \nor its affiliate, except to the extent required by applicable
        law to be redeemable in cash for its cash \nvalue; \n(f) \n\"Control\" means
        \n(1) \n(A) the power to vote, directly or indirectly, at least 25 percent
        of \nthe outstanding voting shares or voting interests of a licensee or person
        in control of a \nlicensee; \n(B) \nthe power to elect or appoint a majority
        of key individuals or \nexecutive officers, managers, directors, trustees,
        or other persons exercising \nmanagerial authority of a person in control
        of a licensee; or \n(C) \nthe power to exercise, directly or indirectly, a
        controlling \ninfluence over the management or policies of a licensee or person
        in control of a \nlicensee. \n(2) \nRebuttable Presumption of Control. \n(A)
        \nA person is presumed to exercise a controlling influence \nwhen the person
        holds the power to vote, directly or indirectly, at least 10 percent \nof
        the outstanding voting shares or voting interests of a licensee or person
        in control \nof a licensee.2 \n(B) \nA person presumed to exercise a controlling
        influence as \ndefined by this [Section 2.01(f)] can rebut the presumption
        of control if the person \nis a passive investor. \n(3) \nFor purposes of
        determining the percentage of a person controlled \nby any other person, the
        person's interest shall be aggregated with the interest of any other \nimmediate
        family member, including the person's spouse, parents, children, siblings,
        \nmothers- and fathers-in law, sons- and daughters-in-law, brothers- and sisters-in-law,
        and \nany other person who shares such person's home. \n(g) \n\"Eligible rating\"
        shall mean a credit rating of any of the three highest rating \ncategories
        provided by an eligible rating service, whereby each category may include
        rating \n \n2 Commentary: The obligation to rebut control rests exclusively
        with the person acquiring ≥10% of the outstanding \nvoting shares or voting
        interests of a licensee or person in control of a licensee.  It is not the
        responsibility of the \nlicensee to rebut control.  This is consistent with
        Section 601(a) of the Act which requires the person acquiring control \nto
        obtain prior approval.\n"

      power to vote, directly or indirectly, at least 10 percent \nof the outstanding
      voting shares or voting interests of a licensee or person in control \nof a
      licensee.2 \n(B) \nA person presumed to exercise a controlling influence as
      \ndefined by this [Section 2.01(f)] can rebut the presumption of control if
      the person \nis a passive investor. \n(3) \nFor purposes of determining the
      percentage of a person controlled \nby any other person, the person's interest
      shall be aggregated with the interest of any other \nimmediate family member,
      including the person's spouse, parents, children, siblings, \nmothers- and fathers-in
      law, sons- and daughters-in-law, brothers- and sisters-in-law, and \nany other
      person who shares such person's home. \n(g) \n\"Eligible rating\" shall mean
      a credit rating of any of the three highest rating \ncategories provided by
      an eligible rating service, whereby each category may include rating \n \n2
      Commentary: The obligation to rebut control rests exclusively with the person
      acquiring ≥10% of the outstanding \nvoting shares or voting interests of a licensee
      or person in control of a licensee.  It is not the responsibility of the \nlicensee
      to rebut control.  This is consistent with Section 601(a) of the Act which requires
      the person acquiring control \nto obtain prior approval.\n"
