      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000030.md
      text: "30 \n \n(1) \nappoint the person signing the contract as the licensee's
        authorized \ndelegate with the authority to conduct money transmission on
        behalf of the licensee; \n(2) \nset forth the nature and scope of the relationship
        between the \nlicensee and the authorized delegate and the respective rights
        and responsibilities of the \nparties; \n(3) \nrequire the authorized delegate
        to agree to fully comply with all \napplicable state and federal laws, rules,
        and regulations pertaining to money transmission, \nincluding this [Act] and
        regulations implementing this [Act], relevant provisions of the \nBank Secrecy
        Act and the USA PATRIOT ACT; \n(4) \nrequire the authorized delegate to remit
        and handle money and \nmonetary value in accordance with the terms of the
        contract between the licensee and the \nauthorized delegate; \n(5) \nimpose
        a trust on money and monetary value net of fees received for \nmoney transmission
        for the benefit of the licensee; \n(6) \nrequire the authorized delegate to
        prepare and maintain records as \nrequired by this [Act] or regulations implementing
        this [Act], or as reasonably requested \nby the [Commissioner]; \n(7) \nacknowledge
        that the authorized delegate consents to examination \nor investigation by
        the [Commissioner]; \n(8) \nstate that the licensee is subject to regulation
        by the [Commissioner] \nand that, as part of that regulation, the [Commissioner]
        may suspend or revoke an \nauthorized delegate designation or require the
        licensee to terminate an authorized delegate \ndesignation; and \n(9) \n(9)
        \ acknowledge receipt of the written policies and procedures \nrequired under
        [Section 8.01(b)(1)]. \n(e) \nIf the licensee's license is suspended, revoked,
        surrendered, or expired, the \nlicensee must, within five (5) business days,
        provide documentation to the [Commissioner] that \nthe licensee has notified
        all applicable authorized delegates of the licensee whose names are in a \nrecord
        filed with the [Commissioner] of the suspension, revocation, surrender, or
        expiration of a \nlicense. Upon suspension, revocation, surrender, or expiration
        of a license, applicable authorized \ndelegates shall immediately cease to
        provide money transmission as an authorized delegate of the \nlicensee. \n(f)
        \nAn authorized delegate of a licensee holds in trust for the benefit of the
        \nlicensee all money net of fees received from money transmission.  If any
        authorized delegate \ncommingles any funds received from money transmission
        with any other funds or property owned \nor controlled by the authorized delegate,
        all commingled funds and other property shall be \nconsidered held in trust
        in favor of the licensee in an amount equal to the amount of money net of\n"

      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000031.md
      text: "31 \n \nfees received from money transmission.22 \n(g) \nAn authorized
        delegate may not use a subdelegate to conduct money \ntransmission on behalf
        of a licensee. \nSection 8.02 Unauthorized Activities \nA person shall not
        engage in the business of money transmission on behalf of a person \nnot licensed
        under this [Act]  or not exempt pursuant to [Article III] of this [Act]. A
        person that \nengages in such activity provides money transmission to the
        same extent as if the person were a \nlicensee, and shall be jointly and severally
        liable with the unlicensed or nonexempt person. \nSection 8.03 [Optional]:
        Prohibited Authorized Delegates. \n(a) \nThe [appropriate court] in an action
        brought by a licensee shall have \njurisdiction to grant appropriate equitable
        or legal relief, including without limitation prohibiting \nthe authorized
        delegate from directly or indirectly acting as an authorized delegate for
        any licensee \nin this state and the payment of restitution, damages or other
        monetary relief, if the [appropriate \ncourt] finds that an authorized delegate
        failed to remit money in accordance with the written \ncontract required by
        [Section 8.01(b)] or as otherwise directed by the licensee or required by
        law. \n(b) \nIf the [appropriate court] issues an order prohibiting a person
        from acting as \nan authorized delegate for any licensee pursuant to [Section
        8.03(a)], the licensee that brought the \naction shall report the order to
        the [Commissioner] within thirty (30) days and shall report the \norder through
        NMLS within ninety (90) days. \n(c) \nAn authorized delegate who holds money
        in trust for the benefit of a \nlicensee and knowingly fails to remit more
        than [$XXX] of such money is guilty of a [reference \nto state classification]
        felony. \n(d) \nAn authorized delegate who holds money in trust for the benefit
        of a \nlicensee and knowingly fails to remit no more than [$XXX] of such money
        is guilty of a [reference \nto state classification] misdemeanor. \nARTICLE
        IX  \nTimely Transmission, Refunds, and Disclosures \nSection 9.01 Timely
        Transmission. \n(a) \nEvery licensee shall forward all money received for
        transmission in \naccordance with the terms of the agreement between the licensee
        and the sender unless the licensee \nhas a reasonable belief or a reasonable
        basis to believe that the sender may be a victim of fraud or \nthat a crime
        or violation of law, rule, or regulation has occurred, is occurring, or may
        occur. \n(b) \nIf a licensee fails to forward money received for transmission
        in accordance \nwith this section, the licensee must respond to inquiries
        by the sender with the reason for the failure \n \n22 Commentary: An express
        trust account or segregated bank account is not required.\n"

    - unit_id: s000001

      body_hash: 3c6e0983ad889dc93334add58721659be3ac3d4bf1075f544bcd9c940396e471
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4/d021ece0cde82565eb83511c8122c85b/sections/s000001.md
      text: 'ey Transmitter License.


        Access to NMLS


        NMLS is a secure web-based system created by state regulators to provide efficiencies
        in the processing of state licenses and improve supervision of state-regulated
        industries.


        To access NMLS for the first time, you must complete a Company Account Request
        Form and identify a Primary Account Administrator and a Secondary Account
        Administrator. This form can be submitted online through the NMLS website
        in the Getting Started section. This form needs to be submitted only once
        per company, regardless of the number of NMLS participating states in which
        you are licensed.


        Within three days of completing and submitting the Company Account Request
        Form, the Primary Account Administrator will receive NMLS login information.
        The Primary Account Administrator will have full rights to access the system,
        submit information to this agency and other participating state regulators,
        and set up other company users in the system. Instructions and tutorials on
        how to access and use the system are also available in the NMLS Resource Center
        .


        Note : If your company already has a record in NMLS, you can omit this step.


        Managing Your License on NMLS


        Each company holding a DFS Money Transmitter License who wishes to manage
        their license on NMLS must create a company record in the system. To gain
        access to NMLS, the applicant must submit a form requesting an NMLS account.


        Current New York State Money Transmitters may transition their licenses to
        NMLS. See the DFS Money Transmitter Transition Checklist for more information.


        Submitting a Complete Application


        To submit an application and ensure your application is received, acknowledged
        as complete, and processed, please follow the instructions on the DFS Money
        Transmitter Checklists . No application shall be deemed to be complete until
        the Department has received all required information, documents, and fees.


        In the process of reviewing and considering the application, DFS may request
        additional information and supporting documents.


        In the application process, an NMLS Identification Number will be assigned
        to your application. Please maintain a record of this NMLS Identification
        Number, as it will be used as your application reference number throughout
        the remainder of the application process. The applicant’s NMLS Identification
        Number must be included on every hard-copy document submitted to the Department.


        Note : If the applicant has already submitted Forms MU1 and MU2 through NMLS
        for another state, the applicant does not need to re-enter the company record
        into NMLS. However, the applicant is required to provide jurisdiction-specific
        information to support its New York State application.


        Back to Top ▲


        Next Section


        Continue


        Annual Reporting


        The Annual Report should be prepared by qualified persons and submitted within
        120 days following the close of the calendar year January 1 to December 31,
        2025.


        2025 NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


        2025 Non-NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


        Back to Top ▲


        Next Section


        Continue


        Reporting Change in Certain Individuals


        Pursuant to the following sections of the New York Banking Law (BL) and Superintendent’s
        Regulations (SR), licensees of the Department of Financial Services (DFS)
        are required to notify the Superintendent of changes in certain individuals,
        within stipulated time frames:


        Money Transmitters: BL 641, 642 and 652-a; and SR 406.11


        These requirements are for changes in certain individuals of licensees whose
        licenses are not managed on NMLS. For those managed on NMLS, visit the NMLS
        section website for New York State and navigate to Company Licenses and Amendment
        under the pertinent industry type, and look under Change in Control on the
        Amendment Checklist.


        Included Individuals


        Members of the governing board such as directors, trustees, and LLC members


        Officers (at a minimum Chief Executive Officer, President, Chief Financial
        Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, and Chief Operations Officer, and any other
        officers deemed necessary by DFS)


        Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Added


        Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized officer
        containing the following:


        Name and title of the individual being added


        Effective date of the addition


        Name and title of the person being replaced, and his/her new title/position,
        if any


        Resolution of the governing board approving the addition


        Personal Questionnaire (PDF)


        Fingerprints


        Background Investigation Report *


        Litigation Affidavit (PDF)


        Authority to Release Information (PDF)


        Resume


        Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Removed:


        Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized officer
        containing the following:


        Name and title of the individual being removed


        Reason of the removal


        Effective date of the removal


        New title/position, if any


        Where To Submit?'

      body_hash: b8cfb71cc698f4b53cce08d023441fce54bf275adbcb1164dfb05a05143f6ba9
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200/6ebc7b743e605b8e05363eb0628942c1/sections/s000002.md
      text: 'How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the U.S.


        Published Date  January 29, 2026


        To get a Money Transmitter License (MTL), businesses must undergo a rigorous
        application process that involves dual compliance with federal (like FinCEN''s
        AML/KYC protocols) and varying state-level regulations. Key requirements across
        states include demonstrating financial viability, often requiring a surety
        bond and capital reserves, passing comprehensive background checks for key
        personnel, and establishing a robust internal compliance program. The process
        is complex, time-consuming, and mandates extensive documentation and financial
        disclosures to ensure the applicant is law-abiding and financially sound.


        Operating a money transfer service in the U.S. involves tackling a myriad
        of federal and state laws, making how to get a money transmitter license both
        time-consuming and expensive. Compliance with agencies like FinCEN is non-negotiable
        to prevent illegal activities.


        Companies can either secure their own MSB license or partner with a licensed
        entity, but legal adherence is vital in both scenarios. It''s essential to
        understand what a money transmitter license is and who needs it.


        What is a Money Transmitter License?


        A Money Transmitter License is an official authorization or money service
        business license that empowers a firm or individual to facilitate the movement
        of capital. This license enables MSBs to handle financial transactions, ranging
        from digital payments to wire transfers.


        Possessing a Money Transmitter License brings forth substantial regulatory
        oversight. Organizations must prove they have the governance structure and
        internal controls to manage and safeguard client funds. States will continually
        scrutinize applicants, denying licensure to those who fail to meet the stringent
        criteria.


        In the United States, the need for a Money Transmitter License is not a choice;
        it''s a requirement for virtually any business involved in the handling or
        transferring of funds. Money transmitter license requirements by state can
        vary, so it''s crucial to be aware of the respective state money transmitter
        regulations.


        How to Get a Money Transmitter License?


        The license application process is designed to be rigorous, ensuring that
        approved businesses are law-abiding and financially sound. Federal and state-level
        regulations diverge, with each state setting its own financial criteria and
        often requiring a minimum capital commitment.


        Applicants typically need a surety bond of at least $500,000 per state, with
        costs influenced by credit history. The duration to obtain the license varies,
        contingent on the business type and the state of operation.


        Money Transmitter License Requirements


        Acquiring a money transmitter license involves compliance with Anti-Money
        Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) protocols. While these regulations
        are federal, individual states often impose additional requirements, thereby
        necessitating dual compliance.


        Subsequent to application submission, state authorities undertake an investigative
        review, focusing on financial sustainability and the applicant''s background.


        Standardized Requirements Across States


        Registration: Initial registration typically occurs with the Financial Crimes
        Enforcement Network or a similar state-level body.'

    available_excerpt: 'How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the U.S.


      Published Date  January 29, 2026


      To get a Money Transmitter License (MTL), businesses must undergo a rigorous
      application process that involves dual compliance with federal (like FinCEN''s
      AML/KYC protocols) and varying state-level regulations. Key requirements across
      states include demonstrating financial viability, often requiring a surety bond
      and capital reserves, passing comprehensive background checks for key personnel,
      and establishing a robust internal compliance program. The process is complex,
      time-consuming, and mandates extensive documentation and financial disclosures
      to ensure the applicant is law-abiding and financially sound.


      Operating a money transfer service in the U.S. involves tackling a myriad of
      federal and state laws, making how to get a money transmitter license both time-consuming
      and expensive. Compliance with agencies like FinCEN is non-negotiable to prevent
      illegal activities.


      Companies can either secure their own MSB license or partner with a licensed
      entity, but legal adherence is vital in both scenarios. It''s essential to understand
      what a money transmitter license is and who needs it.


      What is a Money Transmitter License?


      A Money Transmitter License is an official authorization or money service business
      license that empowers a firm or individual to facilitate the movement of capital.
      This license enables MSBs to handle financial transactions, ranging from digital
      payments to wire transfers.


      Possessing a Money Transmitter License brings forth substantial regulatory oversight.
      Organizations must prove they have the governance structure and internal controls
      to manage and safeguard client funds. States will continually scrutinize applicants,
      denying licensure to those who fail to meet the stringent criteria.


      In the United States, the need for a Money Transmitter License is not a choice;
      it''s a requirement for virtually any business involved in the handling or transferring
      of funds. Money transmitter license requirements by state can vary, so it''s
      crucial to be aware of the respective state money transmitter regulations.


      How to Get a Money Transmitter License?


      The license application process is designed to be rigorous, ensuring that approved
      businesses are law-abiding and financially sound. Federal and state-level regulations
      diverge, with each state setting its own financial criteria and often requiring
      a minimum capital commitment.


      Applicants typically need a surety bond of at least $500,000 per state, with
      costs influenced by credit history. The duration to obtain the license varies,
      contingent on the business type and the state of operation.


      Money Transmitter License Requirements


      Acquiring a money transmitter license involves compliance with Anti-Money Laundering
      (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) protocols. While these regulations are federal,
      individual states often impose additional requirements, thereby necessitating
      dual compliance.


      Subsequent to application submission, state authorities undertake an investigative
      review, focusing on financial sustainability and the applicant''s background.


      Standardized Requirements Across States


      Registration: Initial registration typically occurs with the Financial Crimes
      Enforcement Network or a similar state-level body.'

      text: ', 2026


        Posted in Bank Regulatory


        On May 12, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued a significant
        interpretive letter confirming that Fidelity Digital Assets, National Association
        (the recently converted national trust bank formerly known as Fidelity Digital
        Assets Service, LLC) is not required to hold state money transmitter licenses
        to conduct its federally authorized activities. The OCC concluded that the
        National Bank Act preempts any state money transmitter licensing requirement
        as applied to a national bank.


        Until December 12, 2025, Fidelity Digital Assets operated as a New York-chartered
        limited liability trust company and held money transmitter licenses in numerous
        states, including Iowa. On that date, the OCC approved its conversion to an
        uninsured national trust bank under 12 U.S.C. § 27(a). Concurrent with the
        conversion, the Bank surrendered its Iowa money transmitter license.


        Iowa pushed back. Its money transmitter statute exempts banks and trust companies
        from licensing, but only if they hold federally insured deposits. Because
        Fidelity Digital Assets is an uninsured national bank, Iowa argued the exemption
        did not apply and requested a legal basis for the license surrender. Fidelity
        Digital Assets responded that the National Bank Act preempts Iowa’s requirements
        and asked the OCC to confirm that position.


        The OCC’s analysis of whether a state can require a national bank to obtain
        a state money transmitter license as a condition of engaging in federally
        authorized activities, including cryptocurrency custody, trade execution,
        stablecoin issuance, and related digital asset services, rested on two independent
        and well-established pillars of federal banking law:


        1. National Bank Act Preemption


        Federal law authorizes national banks to conduct a broad range of activities
        on a national basis. Any state law that “prevents or significantly interferes”
        with a national bank’s exercise of its federally authorized powers is preempted.


        The OCC reasoned that requiring a national bank to obtain a state money transmitter
        license, even as a threshold condition to operating, would impermissibly condition
        the Bank’s federal authority on state approval. At the extreme, a state could
        veto federal authority outright by denying or revoking a license. Both outcomes
        are squarely preempted. This conclusion applies to any state’s money transmitter
        licensing regime, including states that limit their licensing exemptions to
        a subset of national banks (such as Iowa’s insured-deposits-only carveout).


        2. Exclusive Federal Visitorial Authority


        Separately, 12 U.S.C. § 484 vests the OCC with exclusive visitorial authority
        over national banks. “No national bank shall be subject to any visitorial
        powers except as authorized by Federal law.” Iowa’s money transmitter statute
        grants the state agency robust supervisory jurisdiction over licensees, including
        the power to demand books and records, conduct periodic examinations, take
        enforcement actions, and even place a licensee into receivership. Applying
        that regime to a national bank would be “fundamentally inconsistent” with
        the OCC’s exclusive visitorial powers and is therefore impermissible on independent
        grounds.


        Together, these two bases lead to a clean and sweeping conclusion: a national
        bank may conduct its federally authorized activities in any state without
        a state money transmitter license, regardless of whether it qualifies for
        any state-law exemption.


        Our Take


        The OCC’s conclusion here was entirely expected. The preemption framework
        for national banks is well-settled, and the OCC’s letter largely restates
        principles the Supreme Court and federal courts have applied for decades.
        That said, one nuance in this letter deserves closer attention: state-chartered
        trust banks are in a very different position.


        Unlike national banks, state trust companies and state-chartered banks do
        not benefit from National Bank Act preemption. Their ability to avoid state
        money transmitter licensing requirements depends entirely on how each individual
        state defines “bank” or “trust company” in its money transmission statute
        and those definitions vary considerably.

    available_excerpt: ', 2026


      Posted in Bank Regulatory


      On May 12, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued a significant
      interpretive letter confirming that Fidelity Digital Assets, National Association
      (the recently converted national trust bank formerly known as Fidelity Digital
      Assets Service, LLC) is not required to hold state money transmitter licenses
      to conduct its federally authorized activities. The OCC concluded that the National
      Bank Act preempts any state money transmitter licensing requirement as applied
      to a national bank.


      Until December 12, 2025, Fidelity Digital Assets operated as a New York-chartered
      limited liability trust company and held money transmitter licenses in numerous
      states, including Iowa. On that date, the OCC approved its conversion to an
      uninsured national trust bank under 12 U.S.C. § 27(a). Concurrent with the conversion,
      the Bank surrendered its Iowa money transmitter license.


      Iowa pushed back. Its money transmitter statute exempts banks and trust companies
      from licensing, but only if they hold federally insured deposits. Because Fidelity
      Digital Assets is an uninsured national bank, Iowa argued the exemption did
      not apply and requested a legal basis for the license surrender. Fidelity Digital
      Assets responded that the National Bank Act preempts Iowa’s requirements and
      asked the OCC to confirm that position.


      The OCC’s analysis of whether a state can require a national bank to obtain
      a state money transmitter license as a condition of engaging in federally authorized
      activities, including cryptocurrency custody, trade execution, stablecoin issuance,
      and related digital asset services, rested on two independent and well-established
      pillars of federal banking law:


      1. National Bank Act Preemption


      Federal law authorizes national banks to conduct a broad range of activities
      on a national basis. Any state law that “prevents or significantly interferes”
      with a national bank’s exercise of its federally authorized powers is preempted.


      The OCC reasoned that requiring a national bank to obtain a state money transmitter
      license, even as a threshold condition to operating, would impermissibly condition
      the Bank’s federal authority on state approval. At the extreme, a state could
      veto federal authority outright by denying or revoking a license. Both outcomes
      are squarely preempted. This conclusion applies to any state’s money transmitter
      licensing regime, including states that limit their licensing exemptions to
      a subset of national banks (such as Iowa’s insured-deposits-only carveout).


      2. Exclusive Federal Visitorial Authority


      Separately, 12 U.S.C. § 484 vests the OCC with exclusive visitorial authority
      over national banks. “No national bank shall be subject to any visitorial powers
      except as authorized by Federal law.” Iowa’s money transmitter statute grants
      the state agency robust supervisory jurisdiction over licensees, including the
      power to demand books and records, conduct periodic examinations, take enforcement
      actions, and even place a licensee into receivership. Applying that regime to
      a national bank would be “fundamentally inconsistent” with the OCC’s exclusive
      visitorial powers and is therefore impermissible on independent grounds.


      Together, these two bases lead to a clean and sweeping conclusion: a national
      bank may conduct its federally authorized activities in any state without a
      state money transmitter license, regardless of whether it qualifies for any
      state-law exemption.


      Our Take


      The OCC’s conclusion here was entirely expected. The preemption framework for
      national banks is well-settled, and the OCC’s letter largely restates principles
      the Supreme Court and federal courts have applied for decades. That said, one
      nuance in this letter deserves closer attention: state-chartered trust banks
      are in a very different position.


      Unlike national banks, state trust companies and state-chartered banks do not
      benefit from National Bank Act preemption. Their ability to avoid state money
      transmitter licensing requirements depends entirely on how each individual state
      defines “bank” or “trust company” in its money transmission statute and those
      definitions vary considerably.

    available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks out).

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance and full
      access to Mosaic''s product set.

      - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic Relay
      holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new markets.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic has pass/fail
      results for everyone but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed at Mosaic''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
      launching close+1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
      Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.

      - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were already
      KYC''d.

      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail results
      exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for users onboarded
      before 2023.

      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
      at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic Relay''s engine
      on day 1.

      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last
      year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

      - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic buys
      Harbor''s assets)

      - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another institution''s
      prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification required? — Not sure
      / need to check with compliance

      - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the last year?
      — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic Relay
      plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its own? — Use/assume
      Harbor''s licenses

      - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what is the
      plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification and recordkeeping
      obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits
      reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

      - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year been reviewed,
      and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed
      and remain in diligence.

      - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what is
      the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before onboarding
      those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses
      for the four new markets.


      ## Assumptions


      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and Harbor''s
      MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition without new
      state approval

      - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s
      own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

      - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and validated
      before close without a monitoring gap

      - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state MTL
      regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in 41 states
      (per the request).

      - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
      which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
      (structure not yet confirmed).

      '

    source_type: workspace
    available_excerpt: '# Harbor 2 matter dossier


      ## Current position


      The Harbor Pay migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned
      Nov 15 close. This is the accepted working view. No decision has been recorded.


      This draft recommends continuing close preparation but making the day-one service
      migration conditional. Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full access until:


      1. Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close service in each affected
      state.

      2. Compliance confirms that Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s know-your-customer (KYC)
      results, or defines and completes remediation.

      3. Authorized reviewers assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity
      report (SAR) history.

      4. Mosaic tests the replacement transaction-monitoring feed and finds no material
      coverage gap.


      If a condition is not met, Mosaic should hold the affected state launch, restrict
      affected accounts, or delay full product access. The $50 welcome bonus should
      also wait for review of its structure, terms, funding, and disclosures.


      The saved material does not establish that the acquisition close itself must
      wait. However, the unread alerts and SAR history could affect deal terms, risk
      allocation, or the decision to close.


      ### Assumptions used


      - Harbor is subject to the state money-transmission and federal anti-money-laundering
      requirements discussed below. The licensing, KYC, alert, and monitoring conclusions
      depend on this unverified legal premise.

      - Mosaic will become the operating provider when Harbor users receive a unified
      Mosaic account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products. The licensing
      analysis depends on this inference.

      - The analysis does not assume that Harbor’s licenses transfer, that Harbor’s
      KYC results satisfy Mosaic’s program, or that the monitoring transition will
      work without a gap.


      ### Record conflicts


      - Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states,
      and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states
      larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says the acquisition
      opens four new markets. The license lists and the intended meaning of “market”
      are needed. Until then, the states requiring separate authority cannot be identified
      reliably.

      - Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`. The reported close is
      “Nov 15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake. A saved hypothetical
      uses November 15, 2026, but that does not establish the actual closing year.
      The operative close date and year remain unresolved.


      ## Decision question


      Does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before
      the Nov 15 close?


      ## Issues


      <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045 -->

      ### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under the
      combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer/survive the
      acquisition


      **Current answer**


      Mosaic should not treat Harbor’s money transmitter licenses as assets that automatically
      move to Mosaic through the reported asset purchase. Mosaic should not start
      regulated services in a state unless it has documented authority for its complete
      post-close activity.


      The acquisition close and the service launch can be managed as separate milestones.
      If authority is not established, the present fallback is to hold the affected
      state launch or restrict regulated functions.


      **Rule and support**


      Saved research concludes that the answer must be determined state by state.
      The review must cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction notices or approvals,
      interim operations, outstanding customer obligations, and Harbor’s license surrender.


      Four sources were retrieved, but no operative passage was selected, read, or
      verified. They do not establish the rule in any affected state:


      - [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)

      - [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]

      - [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]

      - [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]


      The model act is not proof of any state’s adopted law. The premise that an asset
      purchase does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority remains
      an unverified state-law conclusion.


      **Application**


      Mosaic plans to use or assume Harbor’s licenses in the new markets. The planned
      unified Mosaic account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products indicate
      that Mosaic may become the actual provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or
      licenses active might not authorize Mosaic’s conduct.


      Harbor could remain the licensed provider during a transition only if customer
      contracts, funds flow, operating control, licenses, bonds, records, and applicable
      state rules support that result. The documents and actual operations must match.

      still depends on who contracts with users, controls transfers, owes repayment,

      text: '# Harbor 2 matter dossier


        ## Current position


        The Harbor Pay migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned
        Nov 15 close. This is the accepted working view. No decision has been recorded.


        This draft recommends continuing close preparation but making the day-one
        service migration conditional. Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full
        access until:


        1. Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close service in each affected
        state.

        2. Compliance confirms that Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s know-your-customer
        (KYC) results, or defines and completes remediation.

        3. Authorized reviewers assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity
        report (SAR) history.

        4. Mosaic tests the replacement transaction-monitoring feed and finds no material
        coverage gap.


        If a condition is not met, Mosaic should hold the affected state launch, restrict
        affected accounts, or delay full product access. The $50 welcome bonus should
        also wait for review of its structure, terms, funding, and disclosures.


        The saved material does not establish that the acquisition close itself must
        wait. However, the unread alerts and SAR history could affect deal terms,
        risk allocation, or the decision to close.


        ### Assumptions used


        - Harbor is subject to the state money-transmission and federal anti-money-laundering
        requirements discussed below. The licensing, KYC, alert, and monitoring conclusions
        depend on this unverified legal premise.

        - Mosaic will become the operating provider when Harbor users receive a unified
        Mosaic account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products. The licensing
        analysis depends on this inference.

        - The analysis does not assume that Harbor’s licenses transfer, that Harbor’s
        KYC results satisfy Mosaic’s program, or that the monitoring transition will
        work without a gap.


        ### Record conflicts


        - Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states,
        and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states
        larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says the acquisition
        opens four new markets. The license lists and the intended meaning of “market”
        are needed. Until then, the states requiring separate authority cannot be
        identified reliably.

        - Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`. The reported close
        is “Nov 15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake. A saved hypothetical
        uses November 15, 2026, but that does not establish the actual closing year.
        The operative close date and year remain unresolved.


        ## Decision question


        Does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before
        the Nov 15 close?


        ## Issues


        <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045 -->

        ### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under the
        combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer/survive the
        acquisition


        **Current answer**


        Mosaic should not treat Harbor’s money transmitter licenses as assets that
        automatically move to Mosaic through the reported asset purchase. Mosaic should
        not start regulated services in a state unless it has documented authority
        for its complete post-close activity.


        The acquisition close and the service launch can be managed as separate milestones.
        If authority is not established, the present fallback is to hold the affected
        state launch or restrict regulated functions.


        **Rule and support**


        Saved research concludes that the answer must be determined state by state.
        The review must cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction notices or approvals,
        interim operations, outstanding customer obligations, and Harbor’s license
        surrender.


        Four sources were retrieved, but no operative passage was selected, read,
        or verified. They do not establish the rule in any affected state:


        - [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)

        - [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]

        - [source:SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4]

        - [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]

        - [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]


        The model act is not proof of any state’s adopted law. The premise that an
        asset purchase does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority
        remains an unverified state-law conclusion.


        **Application**


        Mosaic plans to use or assume Harbor’s licenses in the new markets. The planned
        unified Mosaic account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products indicate
        that Mosaic may become the actual provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity
        or licenses active might not authorize Mosaic’s conduct.


        Harbor could remain the licensed provider during a transition only if customer
        contracts, funds flow, operating control, licenses, bonds, records, and applicable
        state rules support that result. The documents and actual operations must
        match.


        A partner bank holding funds would not alone resolve the issue. The analysis
        still depends on who contracts with users, controls transfers, owes repayment,
        records balances, resolves errors, and performs regulated duties.


        **Next step**


        Identify the Harbor-only jurisdictions and prepare a state matrix. For each
        state, determine Mosaic’s authority, required filings or approvals, operation
        while an application is pending, treatment of customer obligations, Harbor’s
        run-off duties, and the launch restriction needed if authority is not established.


        <!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start -->

        <details>

        <summary>Saved research and prior analysis</summary>


        Preserved research snapshot. Its facts and assumptions may predate later records.
        Use the current answer above for application to the current matter.


        Do not rely on transferability without an applicable state rule, approval,
        or written regulator position.


        The answer must be determined state by state and must cover more than technical
        change-of-control rules.


        This path is possible only if Harbor remains the real provider and the relevant
        states permit the arrangement. The unified Mosaic account design may conflict
        with that position.


        T'

      text: "27 \n \n(c) \nThe audited financial statements shall include or be accompanied
        by a \ncertificate of opinion of the independent certified public accountant
        or independent public \naccountant that is satisfactory in form and content
        to the [Commissioner]. If the certificate or \nopinion is qualified, the [Commissioner]
        may order the licensee to take any action as the \n[Commissioner] may find
        necessary to enable the independent or certified public accountant or \nindependent
        public accountant to remove the qualification. \nSection 7.03 Authorized Delegate
        Reporting. \n(a) \nEach licensee shall submit a report of authorized delegates
        within 45 days \nof the end of the calendar quarter.20 The [Commissioner]
        is authorized and encouraged to utilize \nNMLS for the submission of the report
        required by this [Section 7.03(a)] provided that such \nfunctionality is consistent
        with the requirements of this [Section 7.03]. \n(b) \nThe authorized delegate
        report shall include, at a minimum, each authorized \ndelegate's: \n(1) \nCompany
        legal name; \n(2) \nTaxpayer employer identification number; \n(3) \nPrincipal
        provider identifier; \n(4) \nPhysical address; \n(5) \nMailing address; \n(6)
        \nAny business conducted in other states; \n(7) \nAny fictitious or trade
        name; \n(8) \nContact person name, phone number, and email \n(9) \nStart date
        as licensee’s authorized delegate; \n(10) \nEnd date acting as licensee’s
        authorized delegate, if applicable;  \n(11) \n[Court orders pursuant to [Section
        8.03];] and \n(12) \nAny other information the [Commissioner] reasonably requires
        with \nrespect to the authorized delegate. \nSection 7.04 Reports of Certain
        Events.21 \n \n20 Commentary: This language is designed to implement state
        use of the NMLS Uniform Authorized Agent Reporting \n(UAAR) process. \n21
        Commentary: States are encouraged to utilize NMLS to satisfy Section 7.04
        reporting requirements if NMLS \ndevelops new functionality to prioritize
        reporting of significant events.\n"

    unit_id: p000027
    locator: Page 27, characters 0–1943
    available_excerpt: "27 \n \n(c) \nThe audited financial statements shall include
      or be accompanied by a \ncertificate of opinion of the independent certified
      public accountant or independent public \naccountant that is satisfactory in
      form and content to the [Commissioner]. If the certificate or \nopinion is qualified,
      the [Commissioner] may order the licensee to take any action as the \n[Commissioner]
      may find necessary to enable the independent or certified public accountant
      or \nindependent public accountant to remove the qualification. \nSection 7.03
      Authorized Delegate Reporting. \n(a) \nEach licensee shall submit a report of
      authorized delegates within 45 days \nof the end of the calendar quarter.20
      The [Commissioner] is authorized and encouraged to utilize \nNMLS for the submission
      of the report required by this [Section 7.03(a)] provided that such \nfunctionality
      is consistent with the requirements of this [Section 7.03]. \n(b) \nThe authorized
      delegate report shall include, at a minimum, each authorized \ndelegate's: \n(1)
      \nCompany legal name; \n(2) \nTaxpayer employer identification number; \n(3)
      \nPrincipal provider identifier; \n(4) \nPhysical address; \n(5) \nMailing address;
      \n(6) \nAny business conducted in other states; \n(7) \nAny fictitious or trade
      name; \n(8) \nContact person name, phone number, and email \n(9) \nStart date
      as licensee’s authorized delegate; \n(10) \nEnd date acting as licensee’s authorized
      delegate, if applicable;  \n(11) \n[Court orders pursuant to [Section 8.03];]
      and \n(12) \nAny other information the [Commissioner] reasonably requires with
      \nrespect to the authorized delegate. \nSection 7.04 Reports of Certain Events.21
      \n \n20 Commentary: This language is designed to implement state use of the
      NMLS Uniform Authorized Agent Reporting \n(UAAR) process. \n21 Commentary: States
      are encouraged to utilize NMLS to satisfy Section 7.04 reporting requirements
      if NMLS \ndevelops new functionality to prioritize reporting of significant
      events.\n"
  - source_id: SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538
    source_version: dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a
    title: '[PDF] CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act'
    extraction_state: complete
    selected_passages:
    - unit_id: p000028
      start: 0
      end: 2132
      page_number: 28
      section_label: null
      body_hash: 80c098d06593529d6d6335e3b8a4fe8e8db356a8c5d82eb34a2001d27d642973
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000028.md
      text: "28 \n \n(a) \nA licensee shall file a report with the [Commissioner]
        within one business \nday after the licensee has reason to know of the occurrence
        of any of the following events: \n(1) \nthe filing of a petition by or against
        the licensee under the \nUnited States Bankruptcy Code, 11 U.S.C. Section
        101-110, as amended or recodified from \ntime to time, for bankruptcy or reorganization;
        \n(2) \nthe filing of a petition by or against the licensee for \nreceivership,
        the commencement of any other judicial or administrative proceeding for its
        \ndissolution or reorganization, or the making of a general assignment for
        the benefit of its \ncreditors; or \n(3) \nthe commencement of a proceeding
        to revoke or suspend its \nlicense in a state or country in which the licensee
        engages in business or is licensed. \n(b) \nA licensee shall file a report
        with the [Commissioner] within three business \nday after the licensee has
        reason to know of the occurrence of any of the following events: \n(1) \na
        [charge or] conviction of the licensee or of a key individual \nor person
        in control of the licensee for a felony; or \n(2) \na [charge or] conviction
        of an authorized delegate for a \nfelony. \nSection 7.05 Bank Secrecy Act
        Reports. \nA licensee and an authorized delegate shall file all reports required
        by federal currency \nreporting, record keeping, and suspicious activity reporting
        requirements as set forth in the Bank \nSecrecy Act and other federal and
        state laws pertaining to money laundering. The timely filing of \na complete
        and accurate report required under this [Section 7.05] with the appropriate
        federal \nagency is deemed compliant with the requirements of this [Section
        7.05]. \nSection 7.06 Records. \n(a) \nLicensee shall maintain the following
        records, for determining its \ncompliance with this [Act] for at least [three]
        years: \n(1) \na record of each outstanding money transmission obligation
        \nsold; \n(2) \na general ledger posted at least monthly containing all asset,
        \nliability, capital, income, and expense accounts; \n(3) \nbank statements
        and bank reconciliation records; \n(4) \nrecords of outstanding money transmission
        obligations;\n"

      text: "29 \n \n(5) \nrecords of each outstanding money transmission obligation
        \npaid within the [three]-year period; \n(6) \na list of the last known names
        and addresses of all of the \nlicensee's authorized delegates; and \n(7) \nany
        other records the [Commissioner] reasonably requires \nby rule. \n(b) \nThe
        items specified in [Section 7.06(a)] may be maintained in any form of \nrecord.
        \n(c) \nRecords specified in [Section 7.06(a)] may be maintained outside this
        state \nif they are made accessible to the [Commissioner] on [seven] business-days'
        notice that is sent in \na record. \n(d) \nAll records maintained by the licensee
        as required in [Section 7.06(a)–(c)] \nare open to inspection by the [Commissioner]
        pursuant to [Section 4.03(a)]. \n \nARTICLE VIII \nAuthorized Delegates \nSection
        8.01 Relationship Between Licensee and Authorized Delegate. \n(a) \nIn this
        [Section 8.01], \"remit\" means to make direct payments of money to \na licensee
        or its representative authorized to receive money or to deposit money in a
        bank in an \naccount specified by the licensee. \n(b) \nBefore a licensee
        is authorized to conduct business through an authorized \ndelegate or allows
        a person to act as the licensee's authorized delegate, the licensee must:
        \n(1) \nadopt, and update as necessary, written policies and procedures \nreasonably
        designed to ensure that the licensee's authorized delegates comply with \napplicable
        state and federal law; \n(2) \nenter into a written contract that complies
        with [Section 8.01(d)]; \nand \n(3) \nconduct a reasonable risk-based background
        investigation sufficient \nfor the licensee to determine whether the authorized
        delegate has complied and will likely \ncomply with applicable state and federal
        law. \n(c) \nAn authorized delegate must operate in full compliance with this
        [Act]. \n(d) \nThe written contract required by [Section 8.01(b)] must be
        signed by the \nlicensee and the authorized delegate and, at a minimum, must:\n"

    - unit_id: p000012

      page_number: 12
      section_label: null
      body_hash: eb065076e15fd657d0f7643c2decce3eaf1414613758d251ef629d3eaa6ad5c4
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000012.md
      text: "12 \n \n(4) \nThe terms of or a copy of any bond filed by a licensee,
        provided that \nconfidential information, including, but not limited to, prices
        and fees for such bond is \nredacted; \n(5) \nCopies of any non-confidential
        final orders of the [Department] \nrelating to any violation of this [Act]
        or regulations implementing this [Act]; and \n(e) \nImposition of an administrative
        fine or penalty under this [Act]. \nSection 4.03 Supervision. \n(a) \nThe
        [Commissioner] may conduct an examination or investigation of a \nlicensee
        or authorized delegate or otherwise take independent action authorized by
        this [Act] or by \na rule adopted or order issued under this [Act] as reasonably
        necessary or appropriate to administer \nand enforce this [Act], regulations
        implementing this [Act], and other applicable law, including \nthe Bank Secrecy
        Act and the USA PATRIOT ACT.  The [Commissioner] may: \n(1) \nconduct an examination
        either on-site or off-site as the \n[Commissioner] may reasonably require;
        \n(2) \nconduct an examination in conjunction with an examination \nconducted
        by representatives of other state agencies or agencies of another state or
        of the \nfederal government; \n(3) \n  accept the examination report of another
        state agency or an agency \nof another state or of the federal government,
        or a report prepared by an independent \naccounting firm, which on being accepted
        is considered for all purposes as an official report \nof the [Commissioner];
        and \n(4) \nsummon and examine under oath a key individual or employee of
        a \nlicensee or authorized delegate and require the person to produce records
        regarding any \nmatter related to the condition and business of the licensee
        or authorized delegate. \n(b) \nA licensee or authorized delegate shall provide,
        and the [Commissioner] \nshall have full and complete access to, all records
        the [Commissioner] may reasonably require to \nconduct a complete examination.
        The records must be provided at the location and in the format \nspecified
        by the [Commissioner], provided, the [Commissioner] may utilize multistate
        record \nproduction standards and examination procedures when such standards
        will reasonably achieve \nthe requirements of this [Section 4.03(b)].8 \n(c)
        \nUnless otherwise directed by the [Commissioner], a licensee shall pay all
        \ncosts reasonably incurred in connection with an examination of the licensee
        or the licensee's \n \n8 Commentary: The [Commissioner] is encouraged to instruct
        examiners to: (1) include all examination requests in \nthe Day 1 letter that
        may require the licensee to obtain records located outside of the U.S., including
        but not limited \nto evidence demonstrating when an outstanding money transmission
        obligation has been extinguished; and (2) accept \nelectronic bank statements
        as provided to the licensee by the bank.\n"

  - source_id: MSG-20260909-982278
    source_label: 'Saved message: From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here …'
    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/conversations/CONV-20260909-a8160f.md
    available_excerpt: 'From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
      close+1.

      Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs from
      the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


      Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.'
    record_revision: e847a82b62c8e0424b39f18d69bdf4564f21aad6b08303affc8f87a05f8782d1

    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/conversations/CONV-20260909-5299cf.md
    available_excerpt: '## Initial issue map


      - **Licensing:** In an asset purchase, Harbor’s licenses may not transfer to
      Mosaic. The four new markets need state-by-state clearance before launch.

      - **BSA/AML:** Mosaic’s policy on prior KYC is unknown. Missing records may
      require re-verification or access limits.

      - **Alerts and monitoring:** Review all open alerts and SAR history before close.
      Test monitoring continuity before migration.

      - **Marketing:** Review the $50 bonus when its terms are available.


      **No external authority retrieved.**


      ## Assumptions used


      - Mosaic will serve migrated users immediately after close.

      - Harbor’s licenses do not automatically transfer.

      - Harbor’s KYC results are not assumed sufficient.

      - The monitoring change can be tested before close.

      - The bonus structure remains unknown.


      Answer saved as a reported fact. The issue remains open.


      Question left open.'

    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md
    available_excerpt: '# Original Request


      From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
      close+1.

      Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs from
      the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


      Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.'
    record_revision: ddeb0f26ab859d90d82d6c6149a6cb045cc5ca0edda3a82db0cb28d68afdaefa
    source_version: ddeb0f26ab859d90d82d6c6149a6cb045cc5ca0edda3a82db0cb28d68afdaefa

## Themis.ai · 2026-09-09T20:53:17+00:00

I've recorded the intake. Here's my orientation to the request.

**Summary of the request:** Dana (PM, Growth & Integration) asks whether the Harbor Pay acquisition migration needs legal review before the Nov 15 close (~10 weeks out). The plan moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic Relay's app on day 1, with no re-verification of Harbor's KYC, repointing Harbor's monitoring feed to Mosaic's engine, a $50 welcome bonus, and unread open alerts/SARs. Dana frames it as "really just a data migration."

**My read:** This is not just a data migration. It raises at least five legal workstreams that need attention before close:

## Themis.ai · 2026-09-11T02:25:42+00:00

**Objective**

Complete the Harbor acquisition and move users into Mosaic’s app soon after close, without launching in a state where Mosaic lacks authority or creating a gap in financial-crime controls.

### Current approach

Mosaic becomes the operating provider after the asset purchase and completes the migration on day one.

**How it helps**

- It uses the existing migration design.
- It avoids a late change to contracts, systems, and customer communications.
- It is more likely to support the planned timing if the open legal and compliance items are resolved.

**How it hinders**

- Harbor’s licenses might not transfer through an asset purchase. If Mosaic lacks authority in any of the four new markets, it may need to delay those markets.
- Mosaic does not yet know whether its compliance program permits use of Harbor’s earlier identity checks without the underlying records.
- Moving all users on day one increases the effect of any unresolved licensing, identity, alert, or monitoring problem.

### Bank-held funds structure

A partner bank would hold customer funds. The bank’s other duties are not yet defined.

**How it helps**

- It could reduce Mosaic’s need for money-transmission licenses if the complete structure places the legally important activities with the bank.
- It could provide a separate regulated party to hold funds and owe the related repayment duty.

**How it hinders**

- Bank custody alone does not establish that Mosaic can operate without licenses. Mosaic’s role in contracting with users, controlling transfer instructions, recording balances, and directing settlement remains important.
- This structure needs new agreements, funds flows, user terms, system changes, and a clear division of duties.
- Those changes could put the planned migration timing at risk.
- The possible licensing benefit is not yet clear enough to show that it justifies the added work.

### Issues that remain under both

1. **Open alerts and suspicious activity report history.** The existing alerts and filing history still need review. Changing who holds funds does not remove this diligence issue.

2. **Identity verification records.** The parties must determine whether Mosaic can use Harbor’s earlier results and what to do when the underlying records are missing.

3. **Monitoring continuity.** Mosaic must show that its monitoring system can receive and test Harbor’s transaction data without a gap when Harbor’s vendor contract ends.

4. **State authority.** Each structure needs a state-by-state analysis. The question changes under the bank structure, but it does not disappear.

5. **Allocation of duties.** Contracts and operating procedures must state who handles identity checks, monitoring, alerts, required filings, privacy duties, and customer communications.

6. **Welcome bonus.** The offer terms and customer disclosures require review under either structure.

**Working recommendation**

Keep the current approach as the planning baseline, but use launch gates. Do not open a new market until Mosaic’s authority there is confirmed. Do not complete the full migration until the alert review, identity-record approach, and monitoring test have acceptable results.

Use the bank structure only if a detailed funds-flow and responsibility map shows a material legal benefit that can be implemented before migration. A narrower launch is the practical fallback if the current approach cannot meet all gates.

The bank structure remains hypothetical. It does not change the current direction or actual facts.

## Themis.ai · 2026-09-11T02:28:50+00:00

The **Current approach** better supports the planned close and day-one migration. The **Bank-held funds structure** could reduce some state licensing risk, but only if the bank takes the legally important roles. It adds work and does not solve the existing financial-crime issues.

**Objective**

Complete the acquisition and migration on schedule. Avoid operating without required state authority. Prevent gaps in identity checks, transaction monitoring, and alert handling.

### Current approach

Mosaic becomes the operating provider after the asset purchase.

**How it helps**

- It keeps the current product and migration design.
- It avoids new bank agreements, user terms, and system connections.
- It gives the best chance of meeting the day-one migration target.

**How it hinders**

- Mosaic plans to rely on Harbor’s licenses in four new markets. Their continued use after an asset purchase is not confirmed.
- Mosaic would take the full effect of the unresolved identity, monitoring, and alert issues.
- A single day-one migration increases the impact of a failure. One unresolved issue could affect all transferred users.

This approach is practical only with launch gates. Mosaic should exclude a state or user group if the required review for that part is incomplete.

### Bank-held funds structure

A partner bank holds customer funds. The remaining operating roles are not yet defined.

**How it helps**

- It could reduce Mosaic’s state money-transmission obligations.
- That benefit is more likely if the bank contracts with users, controls transfers and settlement, records balances, and owes repayment to users.
- It could support access to a market where Mosaic cannot obtain authority before launch.

**How it hinders**

- Holding funds is only one part of the legal analysis. Mosaic could still need state authority if it controls payment activity or has the main customer obligation.
- The structure requires bank agreements, customer terms, funds-flow changes, technical integration, and operating procedures.
- These changes could delay the migration.
- The benefit cannot be measured until the bank’s role and Mosaic’s role are defined.

This structure is therefore a possible licensing solution, not a complete compliance solution.

### Issues that remain under both

1. **Open alerts and suspicious activity reports.** The parties must review the alerts and filing history. Bank custody does not resolve possible past problems or determine who must handle unresolved cases.

2. **Identity records.** Mosaic must decide whether its compliance program permits use of Harbor’s earlier identity results. It also needs a plan for users whose underlying records are missing.

3. **Monitoring continuity.** Harbor’s monitoring contract ends at close. The transaction feed must move to Mosaic’s system and be tested without a monitoring gap.

4. **State-by-state authority.** The legal question changes under the bank structure, but it does not disappear. Each state must assess the activities performed by Mosaic, Harbor, and the bank.

5. **Division of duties.** The operating documents must allocate identity checks, sanctions screening, monitoring, alert review, regulatory filings, privacy duties, and customer support.

6. **Customer migration and data use.** Both approaches require review of the authority to transfer customer records, change terms, and give users access to Mosaic’s full product set.

7. **Welcome bonus.** The offer terms, eligibility rules, disclosures, and funds flow need review under either structure.

**Recommendation**

Keep the **Current approach** as the planning baseline because it best supports the planned timing. Apply firm launch gates for state authority, identity records, alert review, and monitoring readiness.

Continue the **Bank-held funds structure** only as a fallback or targeted market solution. Use it only if a detailed funds-flow and responsibility map shows a clear legal benefit that is greater than the added work.

If the gates are not complete, the safest practical alternative is a narrower migration. Mosaic could delay the four new markets or affected user groups without delaying the whole acquisition.

- The benefit is stronger if the bank contracts with users, controls transfers and settlement, records balances, and owes repayment to users.
- It could provide a targeted solution where Mosaic cannot obtain authority before launch.
**Trade-offs and added risks**
- Bank custody alone does not settle Mosaic’s licensing position. Mosaic could still need authority based on the activities it performs.
- This structure needs new agreements, funds flows, customer terms, technical changes, and operating procedures.
- These changes could delay migration.
- Unclear duties could create control gaps or duplicate work between Mosaic and the bank.
These are new execution and responsibility risks created by the bank structure.
**Issues that remain**
- Harbor’s open alerts and past suspicious activity reports still require review.
- Mosaic still needs a valid basis for relying on Harbor’s identity checks.
- Monitoring must still be tested before Harbor’s vendor contract ends.
- State-by-state review remains necessary. The structure changes the analysis; it does not remove it.
- Data-transfer rights, privacy duties, customer terms, product access, and the welcome bonus remain open.
### Shared issues
Both approaches require:
1. A state-by-state review of each party’s activities and authority.
2. Review of the open alerts and suspicious activity report history.
3. A documented plan for identity-check reliance and missing records.
4. Tested monitoring before Harbor’s vendor contract ends.
5. Clear allocation of identity, sanctions, monitoring, filing, privacy, and customer-support duties.
6. Review of migration terms, data use, product access, and the welcome bonus.
**Working recommendation**
Keep the **Current approach** as the planning baseline because it better supports the timing. Apply firm launch gates for state authority, alert review, identity records, and monitoring readiness.
Keep the **Bank-held funds structure** as a targeted fallback. Use it only if a detailed funds-flow and responsibility map shows a clear licensing benefit that is greater than the added cost and delay risk.
If a gate is not met, delay the affected states or user groups rather than the whole acquisition. The bank structure remains hypothetical and does not change the current direction.
**No external authority retrieved.** The state licensing and federal financial-crime conclusions remain provisional.

## Themis.ai · 2026-09-11T06:24:40+00:00

**Conclusion**

This step is still needed. The saved answer shows that Mosaic plans to use or assume Harbor’s licenses in four new markets. It does not establish that the licenses transfer, remain valid, or authorize Mosaic after the asset purchase.

Do not treat the combined 44-state footprint as available for launch. Make the four new states subject to a legal launch gate.

**Rule**

Money transmitter license treatment can depend on the state, the licensed legal entity, the transaction structure, and the activities performed after closing. The current record contains no retrieved state authority that confirms transfer, assumption, change-of-control treatment, or temporary operation rights.

**No external authority retrieved.** The only saved source described in the record concerns the hypothetical bank-held funds structure. It does not support the licensing conclusion.

**Analysis**

The acquisition is reported as an asset purchase. This makes simple continuity less certain because Harbor’s licensed entity may not be the entity operating the service after closing. This is generated analysis, not a verified state-law conclusion.

The completed intake confirms Mosaic’s intended approach: use or assume Harbor’s licenses. It does not answer whether any relevant state permits that approach.

The existing licensing work therefore remains open. The most urgent scope is the four states where Mosaic lacks its own license. The review should also identify whether the acquisition triggers notices, approvals, amendments, surrender duties, or operational restrictions in any other state.

**Recommended next action**

Commission one written state licensing matrix for the transaction. Start with the four new markets.

For each state, require a clear answer on:

1. Which legal entity holds the relevant license.
2. Whether the license can transfer in an asset purchase.
3. Whether advance approval or notice is required.
4. Whether Mosaic can operate while an application or approval is pending.
5. Whether Harbor can continue operating temporarily after closing.
6. Which post-closing entity contracts with users and performs the regulated activities.
7. The required filing, regulator contact, owner, and completion date.
8. The fallback if authority is not effective by migration.

The practical fallback should be to block or delay service for affected states. Do not rely on a bank-held funds structure unless a separate activities analysis shows that it removes the specific license requirement.

**Material remaining unknowns**

- The identities of the four new states.
- The licensed legal entities and exact licenses involved.
- Whether the transaction documents transfer the regulated business or only selected assets.
- Each state’s transfer, change-of-control, notice, and approval rules.
- Whether regulators have been contacted or filings have begun.
- Who will contract with users, receive funds, control transfers, and owe users after closing.
- Whether temporary servicing or transition arrangements are legally available.
- Whether the November 15 date is still the operative closing and migration date.

**Conclusion / next step**

The recommended action is a state-by-state written determination, not more intake. Until it is complete, the four new markets should remain outside the approved migration scope. This is a recommendation, not a recorded decision.

**Conclusion**

The best provisional answer is **no**: Mosaic should not assume Harbor’s money transmitter licenses transfer through the asset purchase or support the combined 44-state footprint after closing.

Mosaic should exclude the four new states from the November 15 migration unless each state confirms that Mosaic has authority to operate. The bank-held funds option does not by itself remove this issue.

**Rule**

Money transmitter licensing depends on the regulated activities, the legal entity performing them, and each state’s law. An asset purchase does not establish that the buyer receives the seller’s licenses.

**No external authority retrieved.** The outside research call failed. No state statute, regulator guidance, or license record was retrieved to confirm the result for any specific state.

**Analysis**

Harbor appears to hold the relevant licenses, while Mosaic will acquire assets and migrate users into Mosaic’s app. If Mosaic becomes the entity that contracts with users, controls transfers, or owes payment obligations, Harbor’s licenses may not cover those activities.

Having a partner bank hold funds may help the analysis, but it is not conclusive. Mosaic might still perform regulated money-transmission activities if it accepts or controls transfer instructions or directs settlement. The contracts and actual funds flow will control the analysis more than the “bank-held funds” label.

The current record also does not show:

- Which Harbor legal entity holds each license.

- Whether Harbor can provide temporary transition services.
- Who contracts with users and controls transfers after closing.

**Conclusion / next step**

Treat the four new states as blocked pending a written state-by-state determination. For each state, counsel should review the statute, regulator guidance, license record, transaction structure, and proposed operating model.
